Indefinite, so a reminder rather than the reminder. Calling revelation a reminder assumes the content is already partly known and that the failure being addressed is inattention rather than ignorance.
Both words matter. He is a man, not another order of being, and he is from you, so his life and lineage are known and his conduct can be checked against what he says.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Familiarity was the difficulty. In a city of a few thousand, everyone knew who had been a boy running errands twenty years earlier, whose uncle had failed in trade, who had married into which clan. Nothing about a man was hidden, and prophethood conferred no new appearance or voice. The people being addressed had watched the messenger grow up, and that was precisely the evidence they used against him.
studies.didYouKnow: This question appears twice in this surah in nearly identical words, once here and once a few ayat later addressed to a different people entirely. The Quran does not remark on the repetition. It simply lets the same sentence be spoken to two communities separated by an enormous span of time, and leaves the reader to notice that the objection had not changed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ordinariness of the messenger is defended as a feature rather than excused as a limitation. A message delivered by a being of another order could be admired without being followed, since nothing about that life would be reproducible. The passage also arranges its three purposes so that mercy is the destination and warning is only the road, which sets a frame for every threatening passage in the surah around it.

crossReferences.why: Reports the identical astonishment that revelation came to a man from among them, and calls it plain sorcery.
Records the objection in its social form: why was this not sent to a great man of the two towns.
Answers the objection directly, saying an angel messenger would have suited angels, not people.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you dismissed because of who said it: a relative you find tiresome, a colleague you had already filed away. Go back to the content once, in your head, with the speaker removed. If it still holds, act on it this week without telling them where you got it. The point is not to give credit. It is to stop losing information.

studies.title: A People Without Sight
studies.meaning: The entire flood is given in a single ayah. There is no ark-building, no mockery from the shore, no waters bursting from the earth, no bird sent out. Three verbs carry it: they denied, We rescued, We drowned. Then the closing judgement, which is not about wrongdoing but about perception. They were a blind people. Commentators uniformly take this as blindness of the heart rather than of the eyes, since the whole preceding exchange has been about men who looked at a messenger and saw an error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 11 and surah 71 give this account at length, with the building of the ship, the exchanges with the community, and the loss of a son. Here the compression is deliberate, because the surah is running six of these narratives in sequence and the shape they share is the subject rather than any one of them. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An unusual noun that takes the same form whether one vessel or many is meant. The Quran uses it for a single ark here and for whole fleets elsewhere without changing a letter.
From a root meaning to bring something out to high ground away from danger. Rescue in this word is removal to safety rather than defence in place, which fits a flood exactly.

The plural of the ordinary word for a blind person. The commentators read it here of the heart, and the Quran elsewhere states directly that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had ships. Coastal traders sailed the Red Sea, and Meccan merchants knew vessels from the ports at Jeddah and Shu'ayba, but the interior had nothing of the sort and water arrived only as flash flood in a dry valley. A rescue by ship was therefore a foreign and slightly exotic picture to an inland audience, while drowning in a wadi that filled without warning was something whole caravans had died of.
studies.didYouKnow: The flood occupies one ayah here and most of a surah elsewhere. Surah 71 is named after this messenger and gives his complaint in his own words across twenty-eight ayat, while surah 11 supplies the ark and the son. Reading them together shows the Quran deliberately telling one story at several lengths depending on what each surah is doing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denial is diagnosed as an incapacity rather than a conclusion. The community is not called stubborn or wicked in this summary; it is called blind, which locates the failure in what they could take in rather than in what they decided. The Quran uses this diagnosis carefully. It appears at the end of long exchanges, after the arguments have been given and refused, and it explains why more argument would not have helped.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind this verdict: eyes do not go blind, hearts within the chests do.
Gives the account this ayah compresses, including the ship, the waves and the son who refused.
Tells the same events in short rhythmic lines and calls the ark a sign left behind.

studies.applyIt: Ask someone close to you what they can see about your situation that you cannot. Then do not explain, defend, or supply the context they are missing. Just write it down. Blindness of this kind is defined by not being visible from inside, which means the only way to check for it is to borrow someone else's eyes for five minutes.

studies.title: And To Aad, Their Brother
studies.meaning: The second messenger arrives with almost no preamble. He is introduced as their brother, which the commentators take as kinship of descent rather than of belief, since he came from among the people he addressed. His opening sentence is word for word the one just spoken by the messenger before him. Only the closing clause differs, and it is a question rather than a statement of fear. The construction of the ayah itself makes the argument: two different peoples, separated by generations, receiving one message.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were an Arabian people, placed by the Quran in the sand dunes of the south, and their ruins and reputation were part of the audience's own inherited history rather than a foreign tradition. Along with Thamud they belong to the Arabs' account of themselves. Putting them in a sequence beside the flood generation was a claim that local history and universal history are the same history.

keyTerms.note: Used across this sequence for each messenger. The commentators read it as brotherhood of lineage, since each man was of the people he was sent to, which is what made ignoring him difficult.

An ancient Arabian people the Quran associates with the sand tracts of the south. Their name entered proverb: something very old was said to be from the time of Aad long before this surah was recited.

A question built from the verb meaning to place a shield between yourself and harm. Asking rather than commanding leaves the audience to supply the answer, which is why the sequence uses it repeatedly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Aad were proverbial in Arabia the way ancient empires are proverbial elsewhere. Poets invoked them for antiquity, and the phrase from the days of Aad meant impossibly long ago. Southern Arabia held visible remains of substantial civilisations, and the incense route ran past them. When this surah names them, it is not introducing an unfamiliar people. It is picking up a name the audience already used in ordinary speech.
studies.didYouKnow: Aad and Thamud are the two peoples in this sequence with no parallel in the older scriptures, and both are Arabian. The Quran sets them among the flood generation and the communities of Lot and Midian without marking any difference in status, which places the audience's own regional past inside the same account as the traditions they had heard from their Jewish and Christian neighbours.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The repetition of the identical opening sentence is itself a theological claim. If every messenger says the same thing, then the differences between religious communities are not differences in what was sent, and each community's tradition is a version of one message rather than a rival to the others. The word brother matters for the same reason: revelation arrives inside a people, in their own language and lineage, rather than being imported.

crossReferences.why: Places this messenger and his people among the sand dunes, and repeats the warning he gave them.
The parallel introduction in surah 11, with the same brother formula and the same opening sentence.
Describes what became of them and names the boast that preceded it, who is greater in strength.

studies.applyIt: Learn one thing this week about a religious tradition near you that you know almost nothing about, from a source inside it rather than a summary written by an outsider. Not to agree with it. The passage insists that messengers came to every people in their own idiom, and finding out what someone actually holds is the smallest form of taking that seriously.

studies.title: A Trustworthy Adviser
studies.meaning: The charge escalates from the one made to the messenger before him. That one was called mistaken; this one is called light-minded and, in a second clause, suspected of lying. The reply follows the same pattern as before, denying the charge in one clause without returning the insult. What is new is the ending. He does not say he knows what they do not; he offers a description of himself as an adviser who can be relied on, which is a claim about character that the audience was in a position to check.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word he uses of himself was, in that city, a title rather than an adjective: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been known as the trustworthy one before revelation began, and his reputation for it had been established in disputes the Quraysh themselves brought to him. Putting the same word in an ancient messenger's mouth let the audience hear their own knowledge of a man's record as a form of evidence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning lightness and flimsiness, used of thin cloth and a slack rope. It accuses him not of being wrong but of being insubstantial, which is a harder charge to answer than an error.

The verb covers supposition, suspicion and confident opinion. They are not claiming proof, and the wording concedes as much, which is why the accusation and the emphatic particle attached sit oddly together.
From the root behind the words for faith, security and safety. Someone described this way is one with whom things can be deposited, and the word was used in Arabia of a man who held goods for others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commerce in Mecca ran on deposits. Merchants left goods and money with men they trusted while they travelled, with no paper and no court to enforce anything, so a reputation for holding what was not yours was the most valuable asset a man could own. It took years to build and one incident to destroy. To call yourself reliable in that setting was to invite the whole city to check.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this messenger uses of himself is the same one the people of Mecca had used of the Prophet for years before the first revelation, so long that it functioned as his name in disputes. The Quran does not point this out. It simply has an ancient messenger use the word, in front of an audience that had used it themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of credential are set beside each other across these exchanges. One messenger appeals to knowledge from God, which cannot be checked from outside; this one appeals to a record of conduct, which can. The Quran presents both as legitimate and neither as sufficient alone. The pairing suggests that a message is authenticated by the life carrying it as much as by its source, which is why the sequence keeps describing what these men were like.

crossReferences.why: Has the earlier messenger describe himself in exactly these words, a trustworthy messenger to his people.
The king describes Joseph with the same word after testing him, establishing it as a public verdict.
Applies the same word to the angel bringing the revelation, obeyed there and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing someone has left in your keeping: money, a confidence, a task nobody is checking on. Do the reliable thing with it this week before anyone asks. Trustworthiness is not a feeling and it is not a claim; it is a record that accumulates quietly and is only ever noticed in its absence.

studies.title: Remember The Favours
studies.meaning: The same question is asked as before, then the argument changes direction entirely. Instead of pressing the warning, he tells them to remember two things: that they were made successors after the earlier community, and that they were given an increase in build. Commentators read that increase as physical stature, as strength, or as scope and abundance generally, and the word is broad enough for all three. Then a general instruction to recall God's favours, with prosperity as the stated outcome rather than escape from punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were remembered in Arabia for size and power, and their own boast, recorded elsewhere in the Quran, was that nobody was stronger than they were. The argument here takes that boast and returns it to them as a gift received rather than a quality possessed. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits between the objection and the refusal, as the last attempt made before the exchange breaks down.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow behind and to take another's place. Being a successor implies a predecessor who is gone, so the word contains a warning inside a compliment.
From a verb for spreading a thing out and opening the hand. Commentators read it of bodily size, of strength, or of abundance and reach, and the word does not force a choice.
An unusual plural for good things given. It is the word repeated as a refrain throughout one whole surah, asking which of the Lord's favours the hearers would deny.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Succession was how Arabs understood the map. A tribe held a territory because another had held it before and had gone, driven out, absorbed or destroyed, and every well and grazing ground had that history attached. Nobody thought of their land as originally theirs. To be reminded that you are the successors of a vanished people was to be reminded of something you already recited in your own genealogy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for favours is rare, and it is the one repeated as the refrain of surah 55, where a single question about the Lord's bounties is put thirty-one times. Its appearance in this speech connects a warning delivered to an ancient Arabian people with the Quran's most sustained catalogue of what has been given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is offered as an argument rather than as a duty, and it is put to people who are refusing a warning. The reasoning is that a community which correctly identifies where its strength came from will not mistake the strength for a guarantee. This is why the passage names the vanished predecessors in the same breath as the gift: the two facts belong together, and holding only one of them is what produces the confidence being addressed.

crossReferences.why: Records their boast, who is greater than us in strength, which this ayah answers in advance.
The refrain built on the same rare word, asking which of the Lord's favours would be denied.
Names humanity as successors on the earth, raised in ranks, and calls the arrangement a test.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things about your circumstances that you did not arrange: where you were born, a body that works, someone who taught you to read. Then note who held that same advantage before you and no longer does. The passage puts the gift and the predecessor in one sentence, and it is the pairing rather than either half that does the work.

studies.title: God Alone, And Abandon
studies.meaning: The objection is precise and it is worth reading slowly. They do not refuse to worship God. They refuse the word alone, and they name the cost attached to it, which is leaving what their fathers served. Commentators point out that this is the actual point of friction in every one of these narratives: not the existence of God but His exclusivity, since exclusivity requires abandoning something. Then the demand, which changes the subject from argument to spectacle. Bring the thing you threaten, if you are telling the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objection is a transcript of the Quraysh position. Mecca acknowledged a supreme God and maintained many lesser figures at the sanctuary, whose upkeep was tied to the city's standing and income. What the message asked for was not belief in a creator, which they already had, but the removal of everything else, which touched livelihood and lineage together. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A single word carrying the whole dispute. Their complaint attaches to it rather than to the name of God, which is why the Quran's argument with them is so often about exclusivity rather than existence.
An old verb the language uses in only some of its forms. It means to let something go and walk away from it, which names the actual expense of the demand being refused.
The neutral verb for a promise, used here of a threatened outcome. Its neutrality lets the sentence be read as a dare, since they are demanding delivery of something offered as a warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe's gods were inherited property, kept in a household or at a shrine and tied to specific places, seasons and rights. Abandoning them was not a change of opinion; it was walking away from an inheritance, breaking with the men who had held it before you, and telling your relatives that they had spent their lives on nothing. The social cost of the word alone was the whole difficulty, and everyone in this exchange understood it.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand at the end of this ayah, bring us what you promise if you are truthful, reappears almost word for word later in this same surah from a different community entirely. The Quran gives the identical challenge to two peoples with nothing else in common, which is one of the ways the sequence makes the pattern visible without stating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates disbelief in cost rather than in doubt. These people accept the argument and refuse the consequence, which is a different condition from being unconvinced and is treated as more serious. Demanding the punishment as proof completes the picture: they are willing to have the question settled by an event they cannot survive, but not by a change they would have to make while alive.

crossReferences.why: Describes their chests shrinking when God alone is mentioned, and lifting at the mention of others.
Records the Quraysh saying the same thing, that making the gods one god is an astonishing demand.
Gives the same dare in Mecca: send down stones from the sky if this is the truth from You.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you would have to give up if you took your own convictions completely seriously. Not a vice, necessarily; more likely a habit, a comfort, or an arrangement that suits you. You do not have to give it up today. Just stop pretending the reluctance is an intellectual difficulty. Naming it accurately as a cost is the honest first move.

studies.title: Names You Yourselves Gave
studies.meaning: The reply opens by stating that something has already fallen on them, using a word whose classical range runs from defilement to punishment to divine anger, and the commentators record the spread without settling it. Then the sharpest sentence in the sequence. Are you disputing with me about names, which you and your fathers named, for which God sent down no warrant. The argument is not that the objects of worship are weak. It is that they are words, given by people, and that nothing beyond the naming was ever added.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the argument transfers exactly to the Quraysh. The figures at the sanctuary had names, genealogies and stories, all of local manufacture, and the Quran repeatedly presses the question of who authorised any of it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The closing line, wait and I am waiting with you, ends the exchange without a further appeal, which is how several of these confrontations in the surah close.

keyTerms.note: The commentators differ over its sense here, reading it as filth, as punishment, or as divine displeasure. All the readings agree that something has already settled on them rather than being merely threatened.
Indefinite and plural, so mere names. The argument reduces the objects of the dispute to labels, and then observes that the labelling was done entirely by the people now defending them.
In the Quran this word usually means the proof that licenses a claim rather than political power. Nothing was sent down to back the names, so the whole structure rests on assertion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming was a serious act in Arabia. A poet could fix a nickname on a man that his descendants carried for centuries, and tribes took their identity from an ancestor's name and defended it. Words were understood to make things real in a way that a written culture finds harder to feel. This is why the reduction of the gods to names is such a pointed argument, and why it would have stung rather than seemed obvious.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact argument appears in three widely separated places in the Quran, always in the same form: they are only names which you and your fathers named, with no warrant sent down for them. One instance is spoken by an ancient messenger here, one by Joseph in a prison, and one about three specific figures venerated in Arabia.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a test to religious language itself. A name can be inherited, defended and fought over while nothing behind it was ever established, and the Quran treats the gap between the word and the warrant as the thing to examine. It is an argument that cuts inward as much as outward, since any tradition can accumulate terms that carry weight because they are old rather than because anything was sent down about them.

crossReferences.why: Joseph makes the identical argument to his cellmates, that they serve only names their fathers gave.
Applies the same sentence to three figures venerated in Arabia, following conjecture and desire.
Notes that they serve what God sent down no warrant for, and of which they have no knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Pick a word you use in religious conversation that you have never actually defined for yourself. Everyone has several. Write down what you mean by it in one sentence, without borrowing a phrase. If you cannot, that is worth knowing, and the fix is a question to someone who can, not an argument with anyone who uses it differently.

studies.title: Cut Off At The Root
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are given in one sentence and they are attributed differently. The rescue is said to be by a mercy from Us, with a cause named. The destruction is described by its effect, and the reason attached is what they did: they denied the signs and were not believers. Commentators regularly notice this asymmetry across the Quran. Deliverance is credited upward and ruin is credited to the people themselves, and the pattern is consistent enough that its absence would be conspicuous.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This closes the account of the second community in the surah's sequence, and it is the shortest of the endings. The Arabs remembered these people as having been swept away by a wind, a detail the Quran gives elsewhere but withholds here. No occasion of revelation is reported. The compression keeps the reader's attention on the shape of the outcome rather than on the mechanism of it.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, so a mercy rather than the mercy, and explicitly sourced. The phrase supplies a cause for the rescue where the ayah supplies none for the survival being deserved.
From the root for what is behind. It names the hindmost part of a body of people, so cutting it off means leaving no continuation rather than defeating those in front.
The active verb of pronouncing something a lie, rather than a word for doubt or ignorance. It makes the cause of the outcome an act performed, which is why the ayah can attach it as a reason.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs thought of a tribe as a line rather than a population, and the worst thing that could be said of a house was that its rear had been cut, meaning no descendants carried the name. Genealogies were recited aloud and a family without continuation simply disappeared from them. To describe destruction this way was to name a loss that outlasted the people it happened to.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase about cutting off the last remnant appears in four places across the Quran, once of a general judgement, once here, once of a battle fought during the Prophet's own lifetime, and once of another vanished city. It is one of the Book's fixed expressions for an ending that leaves no remainder behind it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The asymmetry in how the two outcomes are explained is the point of the ayah. Nothing is said about what the rescued had earned; a mercy is named as the cause and left there. The ruin, by contrast, is given a reason that lies entirely in what the people did. The Quran's usual grammar of salvation is visible in miniature here: deliverance is a gift with a source, and loss is a consequence with an author.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase as a general statement about the last of a wrongdoing people being cut away.
Names the wind sent against them over ill-fated days, the detail this summary leaves out.
The parallel ending, which adds that they were delivered from a harsh punishment by mercy.

studies.applyIt: Take one good thing in your life that you usually explain by your own effort, and try explaining it once the other way: as something given to you that you then worked with. Do not talk yourself out of the effort; it was real. Just notice how differently the sentence sits when the gift comes first in the order.

studies.title: Leave Her To Graze
studies.meaning: The third messenger opens with the same sentence as the two before him, and then a sign is produced. The she-camel is attached to God's name, which commentators explain as an annexation of honour rather than of ownership in any ordinary sense, in the way the sanctuary is called God's house. What follows is not a task but a restraint. Leave her, let her eat on God's earth, and do not touch her with harm. The test being set is a test of leaving something alone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud lived in the rocky country of the north-west, on the caravan road the Meccans used towards Syria, and their remains were visible to travellers. The Quran never describes how the she-camel came to them; classical commentators note that the elaborate accounts of her emerging from a rock come from popular and Israelite tradition rather than from anything established, and Ibn Kathir declines to build on them.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be separate and distinct, the same one behind the word for the space between two things. A proof of this kind makes a distinction visible rather than persuading by argument.
The attachment to the divine name is read by commentators as one of honour, marking the animal out as set apart, in the same way the sanctuary is called God's house without implying a residence.
A verb of letting go and walking away, the same one used elsewhere in this surah for abandoning inherited gods. The whole instruction is framed as inaction rather than as a duty performed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grazing and water were the two things Arabian communities fought over, and both were rationed by custom. A protected pasture was declared and respected; a well had turns, and each herd drank on its day. The Quran elsewhere describes exactly this arrangement being applied to the she-camel, with her drink on one day and theirs on another. The test being set was therefore an ordinary civic arrangement, applied to one animal.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions this she-camel in several surahs and never once describes her. Nothing is said about her size, colour, or how she came to be there. What is preserved in every telling is only the instruction to leave her alone and the fact that it was broken, which is a deliberate narrowing that the commentators noted and generally respected.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is given that requires nothing of its witnesses except restraint, which makes the eventual failure difficult to explain by hardship. It also establishes that a creature can be set apart by designation rather than by any property of its own, since nothing in the animal itself is described as remarkable. The parallel with the first refusal in this surah is close: honour was assigned by command, and the offence was refusing to accept an assignment.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the arrangement in detail: her drink on one day and yours on a known day.
Calls the she-camel a test sent to them and instructs the messenger to watch and be patient.
Names her among the signs given, and says signs were withheld because earlier peoples denied them.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing today that you could leave completely alone and normally would not: an argument you could let stand, a message you could not answer, something in someone else's care that you would rather adjust. Leave it. Restraint feels like doing nothing and it is not, which is exactly why it makes such a searching test.

studies.title: Palaces And Carved Mountains
studies.meaning: The argument from favours is made again, this time with the evidence in view. They were made successors after the community that had just been described as destroyed, and settled in a land where they built two kinds of dwelling: palaces on the open ground and houses cut into rock. Some commentators read the pair as summer and winter quarters. Then the instruction, which pivots on a rare verb meaning to spread ruin while moving about. Remember the favours, and do not go through the land wrecking it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud built the rock-cut facades still standing in the north-west of Arabia, and the caravan road from Medina towards Syria passed directly by them. Meccan traders had seen the carved tombs with their own eyes and the site had a reputation as an unlucky place to camp. The Quran is describing something the audience could visit, which is unusual in a sequence otherwise dealing with distant peoples.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to prepare a lodging for someone before they arrive. The verb implies the place was made ready in advance, which is why it sits inside a list of favours rather than achievements.
The verb for cutting stone or wood into shape, used of sculptors. It names skilled and permanent work, which is precisely the point: what they built was meant to outlast them.
A rare verb for going through a place causing damage as you go. The Quran always pairs it with a word for corrupting, and the image is of harm done in motion rather than in one act.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The rock tombs of the north-west were the most impressive ruins an Arab of the seventh century was likely to see. Carved chambers with pillared fronts stood in the cliffs beside a well-travelled road, and caravans passed them on the way to Syria. Arabs treated the site with unease and stories attached to it. When this ayah describes mountains cut into houses, it is naming something the listeners had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for going about causing ruin appears only a handful of times in the Quran, and never on its own. It is always joined to the word for corrupting, so the Book never uses it for damage done by accident. The construction describes people whose passage through a place leaves it worse, as a settled habit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Building is not criticised. The palaces and the carved houses appear in a list of favours received, not in a list of offences, and the instruction that follows is about conduct rather than construction. What the passage refuses is the connection people make between having built something permanent and being permanent. The reminder of the community they replaced does that work, since those predecessors had made the same inference from the same kind of evidence.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether they will be left secure among gardens and springs, carving houses from mountains skilfully.
Says they were carving houses from the mountains in security, and what they earned did not avail them.
Names them as those who cut the rock in the valley, in a list of vanished powers.

studies.applyIt: Walk past a building near you that has outlasted the people who put it up: an old shopfront, a wall, a church or a station. Read the date if there is one. Then work out how long ago that was in lifetimes rather than years. It is a two-minute exercise and it does more than most reflections on impermanence manage in an hour.

studies.title: Do You Actually Know
studies.meaning: The elite put a question to the people they had kept beneath them, and the Arabic of that second description matters: it does not say the weak, it says those who were made weak. The question is a sneer, inviting them to admit they cannot really know. The answer does not take the bait. It says nothing about the man and everything about the message: we believe in what he was sent with. The reply from the other side is then blunt and complete, refusing exactly what was just affirmed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the social shape is the one the early Muslims lived inside. The first followers in Mecca included slaves, freedmen and men from minor clans, and the leading families made the composition of that group into an argument, asking whether God would guide such people ahead of them. The Quran repeats this pattern in community after community, which suggests the dynamic rather than the personalities is the subject.

keyTerms.note: A passive form, so weakness is something done to them rather than a quality they have. The Quran uses this word for the oppressed throughout, and the grammar quietly assigns responsibility for their condition.

The mirror of the first word and in the active voice. One group did something to itself; the other had something done to it, and the two verbs are built on the same pattern to make the contrast audible.
A passive participle rather than a title. The question asks whether he is a sent one, which is a question about his commission, and the answer given deliberately shifts to what was sent instead.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in an Arabian town was not only wealth; it was the right to be listened to. A man of a strong clan could dismiss a client's opinion without argument, and the client had no forum in which to press it. What is happening in this exchange is unusual and would have been noticed: men of no standing are answering the assembly directly, and they are not backing down.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer does not respond to the question that was asked. They were asked whether they knew a particular man was sent, and they reply that they believe in what he was sent with. Classical commentators note the redirection: the questioners wanted a claim about a person that could be disputed, and were given a statement about a message instead.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is located in content rather than in personal allegiance, which is a distinction with long consequences. A commitment attached to a man rises and falls with him; a commitment to what he brought can be examined, and it survives him. The passage also shows the socially powerless taking the theologically firmer position, and it does not present this as a reversal or a surprise, which is itself a claim about where such positions come from.

crossReferences.why: Continues this dispute into the hereafter, with the same two groups and the same two verbs.
Objects to an earlier messenger that the lowest of the people are the ones who follow him.
Separates the message from the messenger explicitly, asking whether faith would turn back at his death.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your confidence in something you believe rests on the thing itself or on the person who told you. Both feel identical from inside. A quick test: imagine that person turning out badly, and see whether the belief moves. If it does, you have found something worth understanding on its own terms this month.

studies.title: They Hamstrung The Camel
studies.meaning: The verb used is specific. It means to cut the leg tendons, the standard way of bringing down a large animal, and it is a deliberate, close act rather than a killing at a distance. Three things are then reported in order: the deed, the insolence towards their Lord's command, and the challenge. Bring what you promise. The answer comes in one short ayah, and the last word describes bodies fallen forward and still. The whole reversal takes fewer words than the challenge did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the third account in the surah's sequence. The audience knew the site and its reputation, so this was not a distant legend to them. No occasion of revelation is reported. The Quran gives the punishment here as a violent shaking, and names it differently in other surahs, which the classical commentators harmonise as different aspects of one event rather than as competing reports.

keyTerms.note: The precise verb for severing the leg tendons of a camel so it collapses. It describes a butcher's act done at arm's length, which is why the word carries a coldness that a general word for killing would not.
From a root meaning dry, hard and past bending, used of a stick too stiff to shape. Insolence in this vocabulary is a hardening rather than an outburst.

From a verb used of a bird crouching flat to the ground and not moving. It describes posture rather than death, which is why translations reach for lifeless bodies without finding an exact equivalent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hamstringing a camel was a recognised act with a recognised meaning. It was how you destroyed an enemy's wealth without stealing it, and it was done in spite. A camel was a family's transport, milk and capital at once, so the act was understood as a declaration rather than a theft. Doing it to an animal everyone had agreed to protect was a public statement that the agreement was over.
studies.didYouKnow: Elsewhere the Quran says a single man did this, describing one of them being called and doing the deed. Here the verb is plural and the whole community is named. Classical commentators explain the difference by saying an act one person carries out with everyone else's consent is attributed to all of them, and they treat the two accounts as one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches the outcome to a broken restraint rather than to disbelief in the abstract. What is destroyed is an animal, and what is broken is an agreement about leaving it alone, which keeps the whole episode at the scale of ordinary conduct. It also shows a demand for proof being answered exactly as it was made. They asked for the promised thing to be brought, and it arrived, which the Quran presents without comment.

crossReferences.why: Names one man as the one who called out and did it, then describes the single cry that followed.
Gives the whole account in five short lines, ending on the community being levelled together.
Says they preferred blindness to guidance, and names the punishment with a different word.

studies.applyIt: Think about a small agreement you are part of that everyone keeps by simply not doing something: a quiet carriage, a shared kitchen, a queue. Notice how the whole arrangement depends on restraint and how quickly one person can end it. Then keep yours today with more attention than usual. That is the entire mechanism this passage is describing.

studies.title: You Did Not Like Advisers
studies.meaning: A speech is made to a town that the previous ayah has already described as still. Commentators differ over how to place it, some reading it as spoken as he departed and others as a formal discharge of what he owed them, and either way the words are addressed past the dead to the reader. Two claims are made and both are about completion: I conveyed the message, and I counselled you. Then the diagnosis, which is not that they failed to understand. They did not like advisers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The situation the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) faced in the city was structurally identical, and the Quran repeatedly told him that his responsibility ended with delivery rather than with results. Placing that principle in an ancient messenger's mouth, after everything has already been lost, gives it in the hardest possible setting. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to reach a destination. The verb is about arrival rather than effort, so the claim is that the message got to them, not merely that he tried to deliver it.
From a root for what is pure and unmixed, and for stitching a garment tight with no gaps. Counsel of this kind has no thread of the counsellor's own interest running through it.

The ordinary verb for loving. The verdict is affective rather than intellectual, which is why the ayah does not say they misunderstood or disbelieved the advice, only that they had no liking for the people who gave it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Advice in a tribal society was a delicate transaction. To counsel a man was to imply he had got something wrong, and doing so publicly could be taken as an insult requiring an answer. This is why the good counsellor was so highly praised in poetry and so rarely welcome in practice. The complaint at the end of this ayah names a social difficulty everyone listening had experienced from both sides.
studies.didYouKnow: The root for sincere counsel runs through this surah more than through any other part of the Quran, and it is spoken by different figures. The deceiver in the Garden uses it of himself while lying. Three separate messengers use it of themselves while telling the truth. The word never changes; only who is saying it does.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is defined by delivery rather than by outcome, which is one of the Quran's steadiest positions and a considerable relief to anyone who has tried to help. The closing diagnosis pushes further. If refusal is a matter of dislike rather than disagreement, then no better argument would have changed it, and the messengers in this surah are shown running out of things to say rather than running out of reasons.

crossReferences.why: States the limit plainly: the messenger's duty is only the delivering, and God knows what is concealed.
The next messenger in this surah says almost the same words over another ruined town.
Says he cannot guide whom he loves, since guidance belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone who told you something true that you did not want to hear, and whom you have quietly avoided since. That avoidance is what this ayah is describing. You do not have to act on the advice. Just get back in touch this week for an ordinary reason, and see whether the discomfort was ever really about them.

studies.title: Their Only Answer
studies.meaning: This messenger is introduced differently from the three before him. Each of those was called the brother of the people he addressed; this one is simply named, and the classical commentators note that he came to a community he was not descended from. The charge he brings is stated, and the word for excess at its close is a general one, naming a people who go past every limit rather than one failing. Then the response, and the ayah is careful to say it was their only answer. Not an argument, an expulsion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran locates these cities on the road between Arabia and Syria and says elsewhere that its audience passed the site by morning and by night, so the ruins were part of the landscape they travelled. No occasion of revelation is reported. In this surah the account is compressed to five ayat, while surahs 11, 15 and 26 give the visitors, the negotiation and the escape at length.

keyTerms.note: Definite here rather than indefinite, so a particular thing already understood. The root means exceeding all measure, and the Quran uses the same noun of very different conduct in other passages.

keyTerms.gloss: people who go past all bounds
keyTerms.note: From a root for wastefulness and overstepping, used of spending beyond need and of any excess. The summary charge is breadth of transgression rather than one specific act.
A reflexive form of the verb for purifying. It is spoken as an accusation, and the word chosen is one the Quran elsewhere uses with approval, so the insult states a compliment without meaning to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion from a town was a real sentence with real consequences. Outside the settlement there was no water you had rights to, no protection, and no standing in any dispute. Communities used exile rather than execution precisely because it was slower and left the outcome to the desert. To answer a warning by turning the warner out was, in that world, a decision about his survival rather than merely a rebuff.
studies.didYouKnow: This messenger is the only one in the surah's sequence not introduced as the brother of his people. The three before him and the one after are each described that way, and he is not, which the commentators connect to his having come from elsewhere. The pattern is visible in the Arabic without any comment being made on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The community's answer is the part the ayah frames. It records no counter-argument at all, only a decision to remove the people raising the question, and the reason given for removing them is that they keep themselves clean. That reverses the usual direction of moral language: restraint is named as the offence and stated as though it were self-evidently intolerable. The Quran leaves the sentence standing without comment, which is the sharpest way to present it.

crossReferences.why: Tells the audience they pass the ruins of these towns in the morning and at night.
Gives the same episode at length, including his distress and his appeal for some support.
Records the same expulsion demand in nearly identical words, calling them people who keep clean.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time someone's carefulness is used against them: called precious, uptight, holier than you. Whether or not you share their standard, the move being made is the one in this ayah, and it is worth recognising. If it is happening in a room you are in, you do not have to defend them. Just decline to join in.

studies.title: Except For His Wife
studies.meaning: The rescue is stated with an exception, and the word describing her position carries a genuine ambiguity in Arabic. Its root covers both remaining behind and passing away, and the commentators record readings along both lines without forcing a choice. The Quran elsewhere is explicit that she did not share his stand. Then the ruin, described only as a rain, with no substance named here though other surahs supply one. The ayah closes by turning to the reader directly with a single imperative: look.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran's audience travelled the road these ruins lay on, and other passages tell them so plainly. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage. In this surah the account occupies five ayat because the sequence, not the story, is the subject. The closing instruction to look at the outcome is a formula the surah uses more than once, and it addresses one listener rather than a group.

keyTerms.note: The root means both to remain and to pass away, so the word can name those left behind or those who perished with the rest. Classical commentators record both senses and do not insist on one.
The Quran uses this form of the verb almost always for punishment, while a related form is used for ordinary rain. The choice of form does the work that naming the substance would otherwise do.
From the root for a heel and for what follows behind. An outcome in this vocabulary is what comes after and treads on the heels of what preceded it, which makes it a consequence rather than an event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Household loyalty was assumed absolutely in that society. A wife belonged to her husband's protection and a man's household stood or fell with him, which is why the exception here would have registered as strange rather than merely sad. The Quran makes the point directly elsewhere, using this woman and another as examples that closeness to a righteous man secures nothing on its own.
studies.didYouKnow: The final clause switches out of the narrative and speaks to a single person, using a singular imperative telling them to look. This surah uses the device repeatedly, and it functions like a camera turning to face the audience. What is being asked for is not sympathy or fear but observation of a pattern that the sequence has now shown four times.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Proximity is denied any saving power. The exception is recorded without explanation and without softening, in a sentence that is otherwise about deliverance, and the Quran develops the point elsewhere into a general principle. It also arranges the two halves of the passage so that rescue comes first and ruin second, keeping the order that the surah has used throughout: the ones who were saved are always named before the ones who were not.

crossReferences.why: Names two wives of righteous men as examples, saying their husbands availed them nothing.
Supplies what this account withholds, describing stones of baked clay sent down in succession.
Gives the same exception, adding that the household was to be delivered and she was to remain.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether any part of your religious confidence rests on somebody else: a devout parent, a knowledgeable friend, a community you belong to. Those are real supports and worth keeping. But name one thing you know or do that would still be there if they were not. If nothing comes to mind, that is the useful result of the exercise.

studies.title: Give The Full Measure
studies.meaning: The fourth messenger opens with the same sentence as the others, and then his particular subject arrives, which is unusual in this sequence. Give the measure and the weight in full, and do not diminish people in their things. Two instruments are named, because dry goods were measured by volume and everything else by balance, so the pair covers the whole of trade. Then the wider instruction not to corrupt the land after its setting right, which assumes the land was in good order to begin with.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Midian lay in the north-west of Arabia near the head of the Red Sea, on the route between the peninsula and Syria, and it lived on the traffic passing through. The Quraysh ran the same kind of economy on the same road. This is the only messenger in the surah's sequence whose message names a specific commercial matter, and the correspondence with Mecca's own business would not have been lost on the audience.

keyTerms.note: Two different instruments. Grain and dates were sold by a measured container, everything else by weight against stones, so naming both covers every transaction a person in that market could make.
A verb for reducing what is owed rather than for stealing outright. The Quran uses the related noun for the paltry price Joseph was sold at, so the word names a loss inflicted through a transaction.

From the root for soundness and repair. The phrase assumes the land was already in working order, which makes corruption an interference with something functioning rather than a failure to improve it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A market in Arabia ran on containers and stones. Grain went into a wooden measure, silver and goods went on a hand balance against known weights, and both could be quietly wrong. A shallow measure or a light stone was undetectable in a single transaction and enormously profitable over a season. Buyers with any experience carried their own weights, which tells you how common the problem was.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran devotes an entire short surah to this subject, opening with woe to those who take full measure from people and give less in return. Classical commentators connect the two passages closely, and the pairing shows the Book treating a matter that looks small and technical as serious enough for a whole chapter of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage runs worship and honest dealing together in one speech without a joint. The instruction to serve God alone and the instruction to fill the measure are given by the same man in the same breath, with no suggestion that one is religion and the other is ethics. What follows makes the connection explicit, since shortchanging is described as corrupting land that had been set right, which raises a market practice to the level of damage done to the world.

crossReferences.why: A whole surah opens on this exact practice, taking full measure and giving short in return.
Places the balance in the created order itself and instructs against transgressing in it.
Repeats the instruction and calls it better and finer in outcome.

studies.applyIt: Look at one place where you give slightly less than you are paid for and nobody would notice: the last twenty minutes of a working day, a job done to the standard that will pass. Do that one thing properly this week. The passage treats the invisible margin as the whole subject, and it is the only part of your work nobody but you can inspect.

studies.title: Do Not Sit On Every Road
studies.meaning: Three activities are named in one instruction: sitting on the roads, threatening, and turning away from God's path anyone who believes, while trying to make that path look crooked. Commentators read the roads both literally, as the trade routes where travellers could be waylaid, and as the approaches by which someone might come to the message. The Arabic supports both, and the two readings reinforce each other. Then a favour is recalled, and it is a demographic one: you were few, and He made you many.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Midian sat on a route that carried goods between Arabia and Syria, and reports preserved by the commentators describe its people as levying on travellers as well as turning them from the messenger. In Mecca the same thing was happening in a different form, with pilgrims warned off before they could hear the recitation. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb for sitting down, used of an ambush set beside a road. It appears earlier in this very surah in a vow to sit on the straight path, which makes the instruction here a warning against a familiar role.
A noun for a deviation from straightness. What is being described is not blocking the road but bending it, so travellers who follow it faithfully still arrive somewhere else.

An intensive form of the verb for increasing in number. The favour recalled is population itself, which for a community living on a trade route was the difference between holding a position and losing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every trade route had its choke points, and every merchant knew which stretches required paying someone. Some communities lived respectably on tolls, others on the threat of what happened if the toll went unpaid, and the line between the two was not always visible from outside. A town positioned on a road had a permanent temptation attached to its geography, and the instruction here addresses it directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used in this prohibition and the noun for path are the same pair spoken earlier in this surah by the adversary, who vowed to sit for people on the straight path. The Quran does not connect them out loud. It simply gives the same two words to human beings a few dozen ayat later, this time as something they are being told not to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Obstruction is presented as a distinct wrong, separate from disbelief itself. A person may refuse the message and stop there; what is named here is the further work of positioning yourself between other people and it. Bending the path rather than barring it is the sharper part, since a road with a bend in it still looks like a road, and everyone travelling it believes they are going where it said.

crossReferences.why: Describes the wrongdoers with the identical phrase, hindering from God's path and seeking it crooked.
Names those who prefer this life, hinder from God's path, and seek to make it crooked.
Praises the Book sent down with no crookedness in it, using the same rare noun.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether you stand between anyone and something good for them. It is rarely deliberate. It looks like the joke that makes a person's seriousness awkward, or the plan that quietly needs them not to change. Pick one relationship and check. Getting out of the way is easier than helping and it is what this ayah actually asks for.

studies.title: Until God Judges Between Us
studies.meaning: The community has split, and the messenger describes the split without assigning blame in the sentence. One group believed, one did not. What he says next is addressed to everybody: be patient. The Arabic verb is plural and the instruction is given to both parties at once, and the judgement he points to is said to be between us, a phrase that includes him alongside the people refusing him. He does not claim the verdict in advance. He names who holds it and stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the point when the community in Mecca was divided in exactly this way and the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was repeatedly told to endure rather than to press. Families were split, and both sides lived in the same small city with no possibility of separating. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It is the last thing this messenger says before the threat of expulsion is made against him.

keyTerms.note: From the root for going around something. It names a body of people in motion rather than a fixed faction, and using it twice in one sentence makes the division sound provisional rather than settled.
From a root meaning to bind or restrain, used of tethering an animal. Patience here is holding a position under pressure rather than accepting an outcome, and the verb is addressed to both parties.

The root also gives the word for the bit placed in a horse's mouth, since judging is restraining. A judgement in this vocabulary settles a dispute by holding both parties, not only by declaring one right.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There was no court in Arabia. Disputes went to an arbitrator both sides agreed to accept, often a man from a neutral clan or a keeper of a shrine, and the whole system depended on the parties consenting to be bound in advance. Everything in this sentence would have sounded procedural to the first listeners: two parties, a named arbitrator, and an instruction to wait for the ruling without acting in the meantime.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic says judge between us, using a form that includes the speaker with the people who are refusing him. He does not say between you and me or between you and God. Classical commentators note that the phrasing declines the position of prosecutor: he places himself as a party to the case rather than as the one bringing it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out a way of living with unresolved religious disagreement that neither pretends the difference away nor tries to settle it by force. Both sides are told to endure, and the verdict is placed with someone who is not in the room. That leaves the disagreement standing and removes the urgency to end it, which is a difficult posture to hold and the one the Quran repeatedly recommends to a minority under pressure.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction to the Prophet: follow what is revealed and be patient until God judges.
Turns the same idea into a prayer, asking the one who knows the unseen to judge between His servants.
Instructs saying that God will gather us and to Him is the destination, with no argument between us.

studies.applyIt: Think of a disagreement you keep reopening with someone who is not going to change. Try treating it as filed rather than lost. You are not conceding the point and you are not agreeing to differ. You are declining to litigate it again this month. Notice how much of the relationship becomes available once that one conversation is set down.

studies.title: Or You Will Return
studies.meaning: The threat is specific. Leave the town, or come back to our way. Commentators notice a difficulty in the wording, since the messenger had never been in their way to return to, and they read the verb either loosely, as covering the whole group he is named with, or as directed at the believers among them who had been. What is not in dispute is the shape of the offer. Belonging is being used as the lever, and the reply is a question rather than a refusal: even if we are unwilling.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the pressure described was the pressure the early community lived under. Expulsion from a clan meant losing protection entirely, and the Quraysh used exactly this instrument, including a boycott that cut off a whole branch of the family from trade and marriage. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The correspondence between the two situations is left for the reader.

keyTerms.note: Doubly emphatic in Arabic, with an oath particle and a heavy ending. The construction is the one used for a vow, so the sentence is not a warning about what might happen but a commitment to make it happen.
A word for the road a community walks, covering religion, custom and social order together. Leaving it in that setting meant leaving everything the word contained, not only a set of beliefs.

From the root for what is disliked and imposed against inclination. The reply asks whether the demand still stands with this word attached, which exposes what compelled adherence would actually amount to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A town in that world was not a place you could simply leave and rejoin elsewhere. Your water rights, your trade contacts, your protection in a dispute and your children's marriage prospects were all attached to it. Expulsion was therefore the heaviest sanction available short of violence, and it was preferred precisely because it looked less brutal while leaving the outcome to circumstance.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer given is not a refusal but a question, and it consists of three words in Arabic. Rather than declaring that they will not return, the reply asks whether the demand is meant to apply even to people who do not want it, which puts the incoherence of enforced belief to the people making the demand and requires them to answer it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging and belief are pulled apart. The threat assumes they are the same thing, that a person can be returned to a religion the way he is returned to a town, and the reply exposes the assumption by asking what such a return would consist of. The Quran elsewhere states the principle directly, and here it shows the same conclusion arriving in the middle of an argument, from someone with no power to enforce anything.

crossReferences.why: States the principle this exchange dramatises, that there is no compulsion in religion.
Gives the same threat from other communities to their messengers, expulsion or return to our way.
Asks whether the Prophet would compel people to believe, when God did not make everyone believe.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you use belonging as a lever, even gently: the tone that tells someone they are drifting from the group, the invitation that quietly stops arriving. Most families and workplaces run on some of this. Pick one person you have been pulling and stop pulling for a month. See what they choose when the cost of choosing goes down.

studies.title: Decide Between Us In Truth
studies.meaning: The answer to the threat of expulsion runs through five distinct moves in one sentence. Returning would itself be a lie told about God. Return is not ours to make, unless God wills it, which commentators read as a reservation about the future rather than an opening they are entertaining. His knowledge takes in everything. On Him we rely. And then a prayer, using a verb that means to open and that southern Arabian usage employed for giving a verdict, so the request is for the matter to be opened and settled.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The believers in the city faced exactly this pressure, and the Quran repeatedly gives them speech to hold rather than instructions to fight. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes as the last word of this messenger before the account of what happened to the town, and it is notable that the speech asks for a decision rather than for rescue or for the punishment of anyone.

keyTerms.note: A reservation attached to a firm refusal. Commentators read it as a refusal to guarantee one's own future rather than as doubt, since no person holds their own heart's next position.
From a root meaning to appoint an agent to act for you. Reliance in this vocabulary is a delegation of the outcome, not an abandonment of effort, since one still instructs the agent.
The ordinary verb for opening. In southern Arabian usage it also meant to judge, and a judge was called an opener, so the prayer asks for something shut to be opened and decided.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was arranged by mutual consent and the arbitrator was usually paid, housed and courted by both sides. A man with no clan behind him could rarely get a hearing at all, since the whole system depended on someone strong enough to enforce the ruling. To appeal past every available arbitrator to God directly was, in that setting, the move of someone who had run out of human recourse and knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the densest single ayat in the surah. In one unbroken sentence it contains a refusal, a reason, a reservation about the future, a statement about divine knowledge, a declaration of reliance, and a prayer with a name of God attached to it. Classical commentators treat it as a model of how a hard answer can be given without a threat in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance is shown as something that follows a decision rather than replacing one. The refusal is made first, plainly, and only then is the outcome handed over. The reservation attached is the more searching part: even in the act of refusing, they will not claim to know what they will be tomorrow, which keeps confidence about one's own faith from becoming another version of the arrogance the surah has been describing.

crossReferences.why: Instructs attaching the same reservation to any statement about what one will do tomorrow.
Gives the same reliance in the same setting, messengers answering a threat with patience and trust.
Uses the same verb for judging, asking the one who gathers all to open between us in truth.

studies.applyIt: Next time you say what you will definitely do, or definitely never do, add the reservation this ayah adds. Not out loud, unless you want to. Just internally: if God wills. It costs nothing, it does not weaken the decision, and it quietly removes the claim to own a future you have never once controlled.

studies.title: It Was They Who Lost
studies.meaning: One word travels through this passage and comes back changed. The notables warn their people that following the messenger will make them losers. The town is then struck, and the closing ayah returns the word to the people who threw it, twice in one sentence. The repetition is not a stylistic accident; Arabic reserves this kind of doubling for emphasis a reader is meant to hear. In between sits a line saying it was as though they had never lived richly there, which uses a word for dwelling built from the root for wealth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The argument the notables use here is the argument the Quraysh used in Mecca: this will cost you, look at the people who have already joined, consider your trade. It was a warning about ruin delivered in commercial terms to people whose lives were commercial. No occasion of revelation is reported. This closes the last of the surah's four Arabian and near-Arabian accounts before the narrative moves to Egypt.

keyTerms.note: A trading word for those whose venture came back short. Its use as a threat and then as a verdict is the hinge of the passage, since the same term measures both what they warned of and what happened.

From the root for wealth and self-sufficiency, the verb means to live somewhere in comfort. The phrase says it was as though they had never been well off there, not merely as though they had never been there.
From a root for trembling and shuddering, used of the earth and of a heart. It names the movement rather than the cause, which is why other surahs can describe the same event with a different word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commercial vocabulary saturated Arabian speech. Men spoke of a good deed as a profitable trade and a wasted life as a bad season, and poets used the language of debt and settlement for honour. When the notables call the believers losers, they are not reaching for a metaphor. They are using the plainest word their society had for a person who had made a bad decision with everything they owned.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah describing what happened to this town is word for word identical to the one describing the fate of a different community earlier in the same surah. Not similar, identical. The Quran does not remark on the repetition; it simply supplies the same sentence twice, so a reader moving through the sequence hears an outcome they have already heard.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage handles the question of who is actually taking the risk. Both sides in the argument agree that a wrong choice here is ruinous, and they differ only on which choice that is, which is a more accurate picture of religious disagreement than one where a careless party faces a careful one. What settles it in the narrative is not the strength of either argument but an event, and the Quran presents that as the only thing that ever does settle it.

crossReferences.why: The ayah repeated verbatim here, describing an earlier community struck in the same terms.
The parallel ending, which names a single cry instead of a quake and repeats the same closing line.
Gives the same account in two ayat, with the same warning about measure and the same outcome.

studies.applyIt: Notice who is telling you that a good decision will cost you, and what they have at stake in your not making it. Often nothing dishonest is going on; people warn sincerely out of their own fears. But name the interest anyway, once, quietly. It does not make the warning wrong, and it stops you from mistaking their fear for information.

studies.title: How Should I Grieve
studies.meaning: The whole weight of this ayah is in its last clause, which is a question about feeling rather than a statement about duty. The verb for grieving comes from a root that also gives the word for a healer and for consolation, so the grief being named is the kind that attends someone else's harm. Commentators do not read the question as hardness. They read it as a man releasing a sorrow he no longer has anywhere to put, after everything that could be said has been said and the people it was said to are gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was told repeatedly not to grieve himself to death over people who refused, and the instruction was given often enough that the Quran evidently considered the danger real. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It closes the last of the surah's Arabian accounts, and it is the second of two nearly identical farewell speeches in this stretch of the surah.

keyTerms.note: From a root that also produces the words for consoling and for a physician who mends. The grief named is bound up with wanting to repair someone, which is why it attaches to a messenger rather than to an opponent.
Plural, so more than one delivery over time. The word records repetition, which matters for the claim being made: he is not saying he spoke once but that he kept speaking.
A verb for turning the body away and departing. Elsewhere in this surah the same verb describes people turning from a message, so the messenger's departure uses the vocabulary of their refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grief in Arabia was a public performance with rules. Women keened, poets composed elegies, and a man's standing partly rested on whom he mourned and how visibly. Mourning people who had rejected you and were not your dead was outside the whole system; there was no form for it. What this ayah names is therefore a private sorrow with no social outlet, which is the sort most likely to become unbearable.
studies.didYouKnow: Two messengers in this surah give a departing speech, and the first halves are almost the same words. The second halves diverge sharply. One ends by naming what was wrong with the people, that they had no liking for advisers. This one ends by asking a question about the speaker's own heart, which is the only place in the sequence where a messenger examines himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes seriously the cost of caring about people who will not be helped. It does not tell the reader that such grief is wrong, and it does not describe it as being switched off. It stages a question instead, asked after the work is finished, which leaves the emotion intact while removing the obligation that fed it. That distinction, between what you owe and what you feel, runs through the Quran's treatment of every messenger.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether the Prophet will destroy himself with grief if they do not believe this account.
Tells him not to let his soul go out in regrets over them, since God knows what they do.
Opens a surah by noting he may be killing himself with grief that they will not believe.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have worried about for years without any change. Ask yourself what you actually still owe them, as a list of specific actions, and then do those. Everything past that list is grief without a task attached, and it is worth naming as grief rather than continuing to experience it as an unfinished duty.

studies.title: So That They Might Turn
studies.meaning: A rule is stated with no exceptions: no prophet was ever sent to a town without its people being taken by hardship and distress. Commentators distinguish the two words, reading the first of external difficulty like poverty or conflict and the second of harm to the body. What follows is the stated purpose, and the verb is the one for lowering yourself in entreaty. Hardship is described as aimed at a posture, not at a punishment, and the particle attached leaves the result genuinely open.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early community was under real pressure, and the surrounding city read that pressure as evidence the message was false. This ayah reverses the reading, treating difficulty as a normal accompaniment of prophecy rather than a verdict on it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage steps back from the four narratives just given and states the pattern they share in general terms.

keyTerms.note: From a root for force and severity, used of war and want. Commentators generally read it of difficulty striking from outside a person: poverty, conflict, the failure of a season.

From the root for damage and injury, read by commentators of harm reaching the body itself, such as illness. Together the two words cover what can go wrong around a person and what can go wrong inside them.
From a root meaning lowliness and smallness. The verb describes making yourself small in order to ask, and the same root appears earlier in this surah in the instruction on how to call upon God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religion was largely transactional and seasonal. You approached the gods when the rains failed, when a child sickened, or before a raid, and the approach was made in the posture the word here describes: crouched, small, asking. Nobody needed to be taught how to do it. What the ayah describes is not an unfamiliar behaviour but a familiar one, and the question is only what occasions produce it and towards whom it is directed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for humbling oneself here is built on the same root as the noun used earlier in this surah when the reader is told to call upon their Lord humbly and in secret. The surah therefore names the posture as an instruction in one place and as the purpose of hardship in another, using one root to connect a command and a consequence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Difficulty is given a purpose that is neither punishment nor test of endurance. It is described as aimed at producing a specific posture, which is the posture of asking, and that reframes hardship as an invitation with an uncomfortable delivery. The particle that introduces the purpose is one of hope rather than certainty, so the ayah stops short of guaranteeing the outcome. Suffering is given a direction without being given a promise.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule for earlier communities and adds that their hearts hardened instead of softening.
Gives the instruction that uses the same root, to call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.
Notes that they were seized by punishment and still did not lower themselves to their Lord.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you actually prayed with your whole attention, and what had just happened. For most people the honest answer involves something going wrong. Try one deliberate asking today with nothing wrong: no crisis, no request that matters much. It is surprisingly difficult, and the difficulty is the information.

studies.title: Then We Gave Them Ease
studies.meaning: The second stage is the dangerous one. Hardship is exchanged for good conditions, and they grow and multiply, and then they say something that sounds like wisdom. Adversity and ease touched our fathers too. Commentators read this as the sophisticated refusal rather than the crude one: not a denial that anything happened, but a naturalising of it. Fortune alternates, it always has, and therefore nothing is being said to anyone. Then the seizure, described as sudden and unnoticed, which is what that reading leaves a person open to.
