Gives the calf episode at length, including the account of how it was made and who made it.
Names the same reasoning in another form: we follow what we found our forebears doing.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you have taken up in the last two years because people around you had it. Not objects necessarily; opinions, ambitions, ways of spending an evening. Pick one and ask whether you would have arrived at it alone. You may keep it. But knowing which of your commitments came by comparison changes how firmly you need to hold them.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another
studies.meaning: Two verdicts are passed on the people they had just been admiring. What they are engaged in is shattered, using an intensive form from a root meaning to break something into pieces, and what they do is void. Neither word says the images are weak. Both say the whole enterprise has no substance to begin with. Then the reply, given as a question rather than a refusal, and the reason attached is a favour already received, which commentators are careful to read as the gifts given to that generation rather than a standing rank.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh maintained many figures at the sanctuary while also acknowledging a supreme God, and the Quran's argument with them was consistently about the redundancy of the additions rather than about the existence of the one. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The reply given here compresses that whole argument into a single question about seeking something else.

keyTerms.note: An intensive passive from a root meaning to break into fragments. The Quran uses nouns from the same root for utter destruction elsewhere, so the verdict is not that it fails but that it is already in pieces.
The standard Arabic term for what has no reality behind it, the opposite of the word for truth. It describes emptiness rather than error, so the works are not called wrong so much as not there.
From the root for surplus and bounty. Commentators read it of the specific favours given to that generation, and the Quran attaches conditions to such preference wherever it names one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The images at Arabian shrines were maintained, dressed and provisioned by families who held hereditary offices over them, and a great deal of effort went into their upkeep. To describe the whole arrangement as already broken and empty was to speak about a functioning industry with real staff and real income. It was not an abstract judgement, and everyone hearing it could name the people it would affect.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for their ruin comes from a root the Quran uses in several places for total destruction, and it is an intensive form describing something already smashed rather than something that will be. The sentence therefore reports a present condition, not a future outcome, which is why it can be said of people who were visibly thriving.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply grounds exclusive devotion in gratitude rather than in argument. It does not say the other objects fail to work; it asks why one would look elsewhere when what one already has came from a single source. That makes sincerity a matter of accurate accounting rather than of intensity, and it explains why the Quran keeps returning to lists of favours in passages that are ostensibly about worship.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same instinct, that intermediaries are sought only to bring one nearer to God.
Asks whether any protector other than God should be taken, when He feeds and is not fed.
Says those called upon besides Him cannot remove harm and themselves seek a means of nearness.

studies.applyIt: List the three things you would say your life most depends on. Then trace each one back until you run out of causes you can name. The reply in this ayah is not an argument but an act of tracing, and it works only if you actually do it rather than agreeing that it would come out a certain way.

studies.title: In That Was A Trial
studies.meaning: The address turns to the descendants and asks them to hold an event in mind. The verb describing what was done to them is the one used for driving animals to pasture, so they are pictured as being made to graze on the worst of punishment, which is a bitter and deliberate image. The final clause is the one commentators divide over. The word for trial covers both affliction and favour, so the tremendous test named is read either as the oppression itself or as the deliverance that followed, and both readings are recorded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This sentence appears three times in the Quran with small variations, addressed to the Children of Israel in each case, which suggests it functioned as a fixed formula for recalling the founding deliverance. No occasion of revelation is reported here. In this surah it is placed just before the appointment at the mountain, so a reminder of what was escaped precedes the account of what was given.

keyTerms.note: The verb for driving livestock out to graze, and for setting a price on goods. Using it of punishment pictures people being pastured on suffering, which is why translations reach for subjected or afflicted.
A word that covers testing by hardship and testing by favour without distinction. Commentators divide over which is meant here, and the Quran uses it in both senses within a few surahs of each other.
A particle introducing a past event held up for recall. The Quran uses it to open its reminders, and Arabic idiom supplies the imperative to remember without the word appearing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Memory was the archive. There were no records, so a community's identity was whatever it recited, and what stopped being recited stopped existing within a generation or two. Genealogies, battles and famines were kept alive by repetition at gatherings, and a family that let its account lapse lost its claims with it. An instruction to remember was therefore an instruction to keep something in circulation, not merely to feel it.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence appears three times across the Quran with one word changed. Two of the versions use an ordinary verb for killing, and the third uses a verb specifically meaning slaughtering. The rest of the formula is preserved intact each time, which is characteristic of how the Book repeats its fixed passages with a single deliberate variation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ambiguity in the closing word is not a defect. If the trial is the oppression, then suffering is being given a purpose without being called good. If it is the deliverance, then rescue is named as a test, on the reasoning that people are more reliably undone by relief than by pressure. The Quran's usage supports both, and leaving it open makes the ayah say something true whichever way a reader is currently living.

crossReferences.why: The same sentence in surah 2, with a verb meaning slaughtering rather than killing.
The third instance, framed as an instruction to remember the favour of God upon them.
States the double sense of the word directly, that people are tried with evil and with good.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you got out of that you no longer think about: an illness, a job, a period you would not repeat. Tell someone the short version this week, or write four sentences about it. Memory that is never spoken thins out, and the passage treats keeping an account in circulation as the whole of what is being asked.

studies.title: Take My Place Among Them
studies.meaning: The appointment is stated twice, thirty nights completed with ten, and then given again as a total of forty, which the commentators read as an emphasis on the completion rather than as a change of plan. What follows is a handover, and it has three parts. Take my place, put things right, and do not follow the path of those who spread ruin. The third is a warning given to a prophet by a prophet, and commentators generally read it as covering vigilance about others rather than suspicion about him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentators offer several identifications for which months the thirty and the ten fell in, and record them as reports rather than as settled fact. No occasion of revelation is attached to the ayah. Within the surah, the handover matters structurally: it establishes who was responsible while the mountain episode was happening, which is what makes the calf account that follows a story about a community rather than about a vacuum.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a fixed time. The same word names the places and times set for the rites of pilgrimage, so it carries the sense of an arrangement made in advance and binding on the one who arrives.

From the root behind the words for succession and for a deputy. To take someone's place in this vocabulary means to stand where they stood and carry what they carried, not merely to hold a position open.

From the root for soundness and repair, and the exact opposite of the word used in the next clause. The instruction is not to maintain but to mend, which assumes there is already something needing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A chief leaving his people appointed a deputy in front of witnesses, and the instructions were given publicly so that everyone knew the scope of the authority. Disputes over what a deputy had been permitted to do were among the commonest quarrels in a tribe. What is recorded here follows that form exactly: a named successor, a positive instruction, and a limit, all stated aloud before the departure.
studies.didYouKnow: Forty is the Quran's recurring number for a completed period of preparation. It appears here as nights on the mountain, elsewhere as the years a generation spent wandering, and elsewhere again as the age at which a person reaches full maturity. The Book does not comment on the pattern, but it uses the number in all three places for a span that has to be completed before something changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is shown being transferred with explicit terms rather than assumed. The three-part instruction covers the position, the work and the danger, and the danger is named to the most reliable person available. That says something about how the tradition understands leadership: the safeguard is not the character of the person appointed but the clarity of what they were told, spoken before witnesses and on the record.

crossReferences.why: Picks up the account at the mountain and reveals what had happened among the people meanwhile.
Names the same forty nights and states plainly what the people did during the absence.
Records the original request for this brother as a helper and a share in the task.

studies.applyIt: Next time you hand something over, say the three parts out loud: what the person now holds, what you want improved rather than merely maintained, and the one thing you are worried about. Most handovers give only the first. The third feels awkward and it is the one that prevents the argument you would otherwise have later.

studies.title: You Will Not See Me
studies.meaning: Speech is granted and sight is asked for, which is the structure of the whole ayah. The request is not treated as improper; the answer is a plain statement that it will not happen, followed by a demonstration rather than an explanation. Look at the mountain. When the disclosure comes, the mountain is levelled and he falls senseless, and the point is made without a word of argument. What he says on recovering is a turning back, and commentators read his closing phrase as first among his people or first to hold what he has just learned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the ayah has been among the most discussed in the Quran since the earliest period. Classical commentators broadly agree that the request concerned this life and that the answer denied it for this life, and they treat the request itself as legitimate for a prophet to make. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits at the centre of the surah's longest narrative, between the deliverance and the calf.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to become clear or uncovered, used of polishing metal until it shows and of a morning that reveals what darkness hid. The verb names an unveiling without describing what was unveiled.

A word for something flattened completely rather than broken into pieces. The Quran uses the same term for what happens to the earth on the final Day, so the mountain receives what the whole world receives.
From the root for a thunderbolt. It names being felled by something overwhelming rather than fainting from weakness, and the related noun in the Quran describes the cry that ends a community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the Arabian image of permanence. Poets swore by them, named them as the measure of what does not move, and used them for anything a person could rely on absolutely. Tribes located themselves by them across generations. To describe a mountain flattened was to name the collapse of the one thing in that landscape that had never been known to change, which is exactly the work the demonstration is doing.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah gives what is granted before what is refused. His Lord spoke to him, and only then does the request for sight arrive and receive its answer. Classical commentators note the order: hearing is described as having already happened, and the passage never treats the denial of one thing as a withdrawal of the other, which is why the following ayah opens with a title rather than a rebuke.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The demonstration answers the request in a way an explanation could not. Nothing is said about why the sight is not possible; a mountain is shown what a person asked to be shown, and the result settles the question by scale rather than by argument. The response given on recovering is also instructive. It is not disappointment but a turning back, which treats the asking itself as the thing to withdraw from, without any suggestion that it was forbidden.

crossReferences.why: States the general principle: vision does not comprehend Him, and He comprehends all vision.
Says a mountain would be seen humbled and split apart if this Quran were sent down upon it.
Names the distinction granted here, that God spoke to Moses directly in speech.

studies.applyIt: Think of a question you have asked God that has not been answered the way you wanted. Notice whether the silence has made you withdraw from everything else you were given at the same time. The ayah keeps the speech and the refusal in one sentence, and the man in it does the same. That separation is available to you too.

studies.title: Take What I Have Given
studies.meaning: A refusal is immediately followed by a title. Two things are named as the ground of the choosing, and they are given as a pair: My messages and My speech. The second is what the tradition has always taken as the distinguishing gift here, since being addressed directly is not reported of every prophet. Then the instruction, and it has two halves. Take what has been given, and be among the thankful. Nothing is said about what was not given, and the response asked for concerns the holding rather than the lacking.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran states elsewhere that God spoke to Moses in direct speech, and the tradition's title for him derives from that. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. Its placement is the point of it: it comes directly after the request that was refused, so a passage that could have ended in disappointment is closed with a naming of what is already held.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the clear part of something, as one skims what has settled. Choosing in this vocabulary is selection of what is purest rather than preference among equals.

The ordinary word for speech, attached here as a distinct gift alongside the messages. The Quran names this elsewhere as something given to him specifically, and the tradition's title for him comes from it.
The active participle, so a settled disposition rather than an act. He is told to be among a group, which makes thankfulness a company one joins rather than a response one produces on an occasion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia established relationships and were expected to be acknowledged in public. A man who received a camel or a horse from a chief praised the giver in front of others, and a gift received without acknowledgement was an insult that could break an alliance. Thankfulness was therefore a social act with visible content, not a private feeling, which is how the instruction here would have been heard.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for choosing comes from a root describing the clear part that rises to the top of a liquid, and related words in Arabic name the choicest portion of anything. The Quran uses the same verb of several prophets and of the family lines it names, always in the sense of a selection made from among many rather than a merit recognised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction addresses a specific danger, which is that a refusal reorganises a person's attention around what was withheld. What is offered here instead is an inventory. Take what has been given, and join the thankful, which relocates the whole exchange from the missing item to the ones in hand. The Quran gives this as the reply to an unanswered prayer, not as general advice about contentment.

crossReferences.why: States plainly the distinction named here, that God spoke to Moses in direct speech.
Gives the principle behind the instruction, that thankfulness increases what has been given.
Uses the same idea of preference given to a people, in a reminder addressed to their descendants.

studies.applyIt: Write down the thing you most wanted this year and did not get. Then, underneath, list what you did get in the same period. Do not compare them or draw a conclusion. Just have both lists in front of you at once. The ayah's whole method is to put an inventory next to a refusal and let the reader look at the page.

studies.title: Take The Best Of It
studies.meaning: What was inscribed is described in two words that sit oddly together: admonition, which moves a person, and detailed setting-out, which informs them. Then the instruction, take it with strength, using a word for firmness of grip. The last clause is the one commentators divide over. Tell your people to take the best of it: either the best of what is in it, preferring pardon to retaliation and patience to response, or all of it, since all of it is best. Both readings are old and neither is treated as excluding the other.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran does not describe the tablets' material or number and classical commentators note that the details reported about them come from Israelite tradition rather than from anything established. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It comes directly after the naming of what was given, so the record follows the title, and the closing promise about seeing the abode of the transgressors turns the passage forward.

keyTerms.note: The plural of an ordinary word for a plank or flat board. The Quran uses the same word for the timbers of a ship and, in the singular, for the preserved tablet, so it covers a range from carpentry upward.
From a root for counsel that softens a hearer and moves them to change. It names the effect rather than the content, which is why it is paired here with a second word describing information.
A superlative with a possessive ending. Commentators read it either as choosing the finer option among what is permitted, or as taking the whole because every part of it is best.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Arabia and was rare. A few men in Mecca could write, contracts were occasionally recorded, and a written document carried enormous weight precisely because almost everything else was held in memory. To hear of a revelation inscribed and handed over as an object was to hear of a permanence that recitation, however carefully preserved, did not visibly have.
studies.didYouKnow: One ordinary Arabic word for a flat board does three jobs in the Quran. It names the planks of the ship built before the flood, the tablets given at the mountain, and the preserved tablet on which the Book is described as written. The same everyday noun a carpenter would use covers a hull, a scripture and something in the unseen.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing of admonition and detail describes a revelation that works on two levels at once, moving a person and informing them, with neither reducible to the other. The instruction to hold it with strength assumes a grip that can loosen. And whichever reading of the closing clause is taken, both leave the reader with a task of discernment, since even taking all of it requires knowing which part applies to the situation in front of you.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a tablet, describing the Quran as in a preserved one.
Applies the same word to the planks of the ship carried through the flood.
Gives the same instruction to this community, to follow the best of what was sent down.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you know you should do and ask what the best version of it looks like, rather than the acceptable one. Usually the gap is small: a message sent rather than thought about, an apology without the qualifier. Do the better version once today. That is the whole of what the closing instruction asks for, at the scale it is actually met.

studies.title: Every Sign They See
studies.meaning: Three conditional clauses run in a row and they describe a settled orientation rather than a series of mistakes. Every sign is seen and not believed; the road of sound judgement is seen and not taken; the road of going wrong is seen and taken. The word for sound judgement means the maturity that lets a person handle their own affairs, and its opposite means wandering off. The reason given at the end is the same one given ten ayat earlier, word for word, and it names denial and heedlessness together.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh objection to the message was tangled with their standing, and the Quran repeatedly describes their refusal in terms of self-importance rather than of evidence. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It stands between the account of the tablets and the account of the calf, generalising from one narrative before the surah returns to the next episode of it.

keyTerms.note: The same reflexive verb used of the first refusal at the start of this surah. The grammar carries the falseness inside the word, since it means treating oneself as great rather than being so.

The word for the maturity at which a person can be trusted with their own affairs. It names competence in living rather than correctness of belief, which is a more practical idea than guidance in the abstract.
Its standard opposite in Arabic, naming the state of one who wanders without direction. Another surah places the two words together in a single famous sentence about clarity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in Arabia were choices, not surfaces. A traveller at a junction picked between routes on the advice of a guide, and taking the wrong one could mean days without water. Everyone had the experience of seeing the right way and being talked out of it, or of following a track because it was easier underfoot. The vocabulary of two roads was therefore literal before it was moral.
studies.didYouKnow: The reason clause that closes this ayah is identical, word for word, to the one that closes an ayah ten places earlier in the same surah, where it explains the drowning. The Quran repeats the whole phrase without variation, so the same two failures, denial and heedlessness, are given as the cause in two quite different settings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three clauses describe a condition that argument cannot reach, since seeing is not what is missing in any of them. The passage names the cause as self-magnifying without right, which locates the problem in a posture rather than in a belief. And it is careful about sequence, giving the denial as the reason for the turning away rather than the other way round, which keeps the description from being about people who were never given a chance.

crossReferences.why: Places the same two words together, saying that right direction has become clear from error.
Ends with the identical reason clause, applied there to a completely different community.
Describes hearts and sight being turned about, as they refused to believe the first time.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you know is better for you and have not started, where the reason is not doubt. Usually it is a small dignity: it would mean admitting you were wrong, or being a beginner in front of people. Name the dignity out loud. It is almost always smaller than what it is costing you, and saying it makes that visible.

studies.title: Their Works Came To Nothing
studies.meaning: Two denials are named together, the signs and the meeting that comes after, and the outcome is given with a verb that Arabic lexicographers explain from grazing. An animal that eats too much of a certain plant swells and then dies of it, and the same verb describes works that grow impressively and are worthless. Nothing is said about the deeds being few or badly done. Then a question closes the ayah, and it removes any suggestion of an added penalty. They receive what they were doing, and nothing beyond it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh performed real acts of generosity, fed pilgrims, maintained the sanctuary and kept oaths, and they regarded these as their standing before God. The Quran addresses them not by denying the acts but by asking what the acts were oriented towards. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It comes in a run of general statements between two stages of one narrative.

keyTerms.note: Lexicographers explain the verb from an animal that grazes greedily on a plant, swells up and dies. It describes something that looks like abundance and is in fact the shape of a loss.
The ordinary noun for an encounter. Naming the hereafter as a meeting rather than a place makes what is denied a personal appointment rather than a doctrine about geography.
From the root for settling an account and paying what is due. The question at the end uses it to rule out anything extra, so the outcome is described as an exact settlement rather than a sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herdsmen knew the plants that bloated a beast, and they knew that a swollen animal was not a fat one. The distinction between a herd that had grown and a herd that was dying looked identical for a day or two and was completely different underneath. This is the picture the verb carries, and to a people who lived off animals it named a specific and familiar kind of ruinous appearance.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the Quran uses for the hereafter in this ayah is simply the word for a meeting. The Book repeatedly describes what comes after death in the language of an appointment kept or missed rather than of a location entered, and denial of it is phrased throughout as denying an encounter rather than as denying a place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the quantity of what a person does from what it is oriented towards. Deeds do not vanish because they were insufficient; they are described as swelling and coming to nothing, which is a statement about direction rather than about volume. The closing question protects the reader from reading this as vindictiveness. Nothing is added. What is described is simply an account settled at its real value.

crossReferences.why: Describes deeds turned into scattered dust, a matching image for effort that had nothing behind it.
Names those whose striving in this life was lost while they reckoned they were doing well.
Compares the deeds of the disbelievers to a mirage a thirsty man takes for water.

studies.applyIt: Look at the thing you have put the most hours into this year and ask what it is ultimately for. Not the immediate purpose, the one after that. If you cannot get past two answers, that is worth sitting with. The ayah is not about doing less. It is about knowing what the effort is pointed at.

studies.title: A Body That Lowed
studies.meaning: The description is careful not to concede anything. It was made from their own ornaments, and what it was is given as a body with a lowing, using a word the Quran reserves for forms without life. Nothing is said about it moving or acting. Then two questions, and they are the two tests that matter in this narrative. Did they not see that it does not speak to them, and does not guide them to any road. Those are precisely the two things the Lord they had just left behind had done.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The episode is given here in five ayat while another surah supplies the account of who made it and how. No occasion of revelation is reported. The placement within this surah is the point: the request for a made god was voiced only ten ayat earlier, immediately after the crossing of the sea, and here that same request is satisfied by the people themselves during a forty-night absence.

keyTerms.note: The jewellery they were carrying, which they had brought out of Egypt with them. The material of the object is named first, before anything about its form, which keeps its origin in view throughout.

The Quran uses this word for forms that lack life or ordinary need. Choosing it here denies animation before any question about the object is raised, so the description settles the matter in one word.
The specific noun for the sound a cow makes. The ayah grants it a noise and nothing else, and the two questions that follow ask about speech and direction, which a noise is not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gold in that world was worn rather than banked. A family's wealth hung on its women, and it moved with them, which is why a fleeing population carried its capital as ornament. Melting that down was therefore not an act of piety funded from a treasury. It was a community spending its entire portable estate, all at once, on an object that made a sound.
studies.didYouKnow: The two tests named here answer directly to the two things reported of God in the preceding ayat of this same surah. He had spoken, at the mountain, and He had guided them, through the sea. The object is measured against exactly those two functions and fails both, and the surah arranges the ayat so that the comparison is available without being stated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran's argument here is not that the object was weak but that it was mute. Speech and direction are named as the two things that make a relationship possible, since one addresses you and the other takes you somewhere, and an object that offers neither cannot be in a relationship with anyone. That criterion is portable. It applies to anything a person orients a life around, and most such things also do not speak.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, which asks the same question, seeing that it returned them no word.
The request made ten ayat earlier for a god to be made for them, using the same verb.
Abraham asks the same kind of question of objects that neither benefit nor harm those who serve them.

studies.applyIt: Apply the two tests to something you organise your week around. Does it say anything back to you, and does it take you somewhere. Plenty of good things fail one and pass the other. What the ayah is watching for is the thing that fails both and still holds the centre of a life, which is easier to acquire than anyone expects.

studies.title: When It Fell Into Their Hands
studies.meaning: The Arabic for their remorse is a phrase found nowhere else in the Book, and its literal sense is that it was dropped into their hands. Grammarians have discussed it for centuries as an image of regret so physical it is felt in the body. Two things happen together, the regret and the seeing, and the seeing is put second. Only after the feeling arrives do they recognise what they had done. The words they then speak are almost exactly the words spoken by the first human beings, with two verbs exchanged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The expression here entered Arabic largely through this ayah, and classical lexicographers cite it as an example of an idiom the Quran gave the language. No occasion of revelation is reported. Within the surah the passage sits between the making of the calf and the return from the mountain, so the community's remorse is recorded before anyone arrives to confront them with it.

keyTerms.gloss: it was dropped into their hands
keyTerms.note: A passive construction found only here in the Quran. Lexicographers explain it as the bodily feel of remorse, the sinking that arrives before any thought about it, and Arabic keeps the idiom to this day.
The verb for losing one's road. It is placed after the feeling rather than before it, so the passage describes people who felt something was wrong and only then worked out what.
An emphatic conditional used for a case treated as serious rather than hypothetical. The sentence it opens states an outcome without asking to be spared it, which is what makes the plea unusual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic had a whole vocabulary of gesture for remorse: biting the hand, striking one palm on the other, letting the hands fall open. Poets used these instead of naming the feeling, because the audience read the body before it read the word. The idiom in this ayah belongs to that repertoire, which is why it works without any abstract noun for regret appearing in the sentence at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The plea in this ayah is the same sentence spoken by the first human beings earlier in this same surah, with the two central verbs in reverse order. There it is forgiveness then mercy, spoken in the second person to God directly. Here it is mercy then forgiveness, spoken in the third person about Him. The closing clause is word for word identical.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Recognition is described as arriving after the feeling rather than producing it, which reverses the order most people assume. The passage also gives the community the same words as the first parents, which places an act of collective idolatry and a single slip under the same form of response. Nothing in the plea bargains, explains, or asks to be excused. It states a dependence and a consequence, and stops.

crossReferences.why: The same plea earlier in this surah, with the words for forgiveness and mercy in the other order.
Gives what happened before this moment, the people refusing to leave the calf until Moses returned.
Shows the same gesture of regret, a man biting his hands over what he chose.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you feel regret before you can name it: the tightening when a message arrives, the reluctance to open a particular drawer. That signal is usually accurate and usually ignored for weeks. Follow one of them this week to whatever it is attached to, and do not decide anything until you have found out what it was pointing at.

studies.title: Son Of My Mother
studies.meaning: Two words describe the state he returns in, and commentators note that the second covers both fury and grief, so the Arabic does not make the reader choose. What follows is described plainly and without softening: he casts down the tablets and takes his brother by the head, pulling him close. The reply is where the ayah turns. It opens by naming their shared mother, not their shared father, appealing to the tenderest available bond, and then asks for two things: not to be made a spectacle for enemies, and not to be counted among the wrongdoers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this scene in two surahs and neither of them says the tablets broke; one says they were cast down and the other says they were taken up again when the anger subsided. The details about breakage circulating in the commentaries come from Israelite tradition, which classical authorities identify as such. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: Commentators record both senses for this word and it carries them together here. Anger and grief share a form in Arabic because they share an occasion, which is caring about something that has been damaged.
They shared both parents, so naming the mother is a choice. Arabic uses the maternal bond where an appeal needs tenderness rather than authority, and the vocative form here is unusually intimate.
From a root naming the specific pleasure taken in an enemy's misfortune. English has no single word for it. The request is not to be spared harm but not to become the occasion of that pleasure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Brothers in Arabia were expected to hold together absolutely, and a quarrel between them in public was a gift to a rival clan. Half-brothers by different mothers were common in a society with plural marriage, and the phrase son of my mother marked the closest possible tie, the one that did not depend on inheritance or clan politics. It was the word you used when you needed to be heard as family rather than as a colleague.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes the tablets being thrown down and, four ayat later, being picked up again when the anger settled. Neither passage says they broke or that anything was lost. Classical commentators note that the accounts of breakage come from Israelite tradition rather than from the Book, and Ibn Kathir treats them as reports rather than as established.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a prophet in a state of overwhelming anger and does not tidy it away. What it does instead is show the exchange completing: the brother speaks, the appeal lands, and the next ayah is a prayer for both of them. That sequence is the point. Anger is not presented as disqualifying, and the repair is shown taking place in the next breath rather than being deferred or narrated away.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, where the same plea mentions the beard and the fear of causing division.
The immediate answer, a prayer asking forgiveness for himself first and then his brother.
Shows the other end of a sibling rupture, forgiveness given without any account being settled.

studies.applyIt: If you are in the middle of something with a sibling or a close relative, try the move the brother makes here. Do not defend the facts first. Name the relationship, then say what you are actually afraid of. It takes one sentence and it changes what the other person is answering, which is the only part you can control.

studies.title: Forgive Me And My Brother
studies.meaning: The order is the striking thing. He asks forgiveness for himself before his brother, although he is the one who has just seized the other by the head and his brother is the one who was overpowered. Commentators regularly note the sequence. Then the second request uses a verb of entry, so mercy is asked for as a space to be admitted into rather than as a quality to receive. The closing phrase is a superlative built on the same root twice, naming God as the most merciful of all who show mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately following the confrontation between the two brothers. No occasion of revelation is reported. The same closing phrase appears elsewhere in the Quran as the last words of Job's petition from long affliction, and in the Joseph account at a moment of extreme grief, so the surah is using a formula the Book reserves for people who have nothing left to argue with.

keyTerms.note: The self comes first in the sentence, before the brother. Classical commentators note the order and read it as a man beginning where the responsibility is nearest before extending the prayer outward.
A verb of entering, so mercy is asked for as a place with an inside rather than as something handed over. The Quran uses the same construction elsewhere for entering God's servants and His garden.
A superlative formed from the root repeated twice. It does not say God is merciful and others are not; it places Him at the top of a scale that includes every merciful being.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was entered rather than received. A man in danger went to a stronger house and asked to be taken in, and once admitted he was under that household's guarantee against everyone. The formula was spoken aloud and witnessed. Asking to be admitted into mercy would have carried that whole picture: not a gift handed over at the door but a threshold crossed, with everything on the other side of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes this prayer appears at only a few points in the Quran, and each time in the mouth of someone at the end of what they can bear. Job uses it after long affliction, and it appears in the Joseph account at a moment of grief. The formula is reserved, and the Book does not spread it across ordinary petitions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer models an order that runs against instinct. A person who has just been in the right, or has just acted from a defensible motive, asks first for himself, which treats even justified anger as something to bring for forgiveness rather than to defend. And by asking for both of them together in one clause, the petition repairs the rupture inside the prayer itself, before anything else is said about it.

crossReferences.why: Job's petition ends with the same phrase, after describing affliction without asking for anything specific.
Jacob uses the same words when he has run out of grounds for confidence in anyone else.
Abraham's prayer asks forgiveness for himself, his parents and the believers, in a widening order.

studies.applyIt: The next time you have been wronged and also lost your temper, try praying for yourself first. Not because your grievance was invalid. Because starting with the part that is yours is the only place a repair can actually begin, and it removes the need to establish who was more at fault before anything can move.

studies.title: Then Repented Afterwards
studies.meaning: Two ayat placed side by side, and they are not in tension. The first names a consequence for those who took the calf, wrath and lowliness in this life, and generalises it to those who fabricate. The second gives the other track: those who did wrong, then turned back after it, and believed. The Arabic phrase meaning after that appears twice in the short second ayah, once for their turning and once for God's response, so the grammar puts His answer in the same position after their move that their move occupied after the wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran repeatedly places a statement of consequence directly beside a statement of mercy, and neither is allowed to cancel the other. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. Their position in the surah matters: the community has already been shown regretting, several ayat earlier, so the reader meets the opening of the door after having watched people arrive at it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being made small and submissive, used of a path worn down by feet. It names a public condition in this life, placed alongside a consequence that belongs to the next.
From the root for cutting leather to a pattern. The general rule is stated of fabricators rather than of that community, which lifts the ayah out of one episode into a class of conduct.
The same phrase occurs twice in the second ayah, first of their turning and then of God's response. The repetition makes the answer follow their move in exactly the way their move followed the wrong.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Restoration after disgrace was possible in Arabian society but slow and public. A man who had broken faith regained standing by conduct witnessed over years, and the community decided when the account was closed rather than the individual. Against that background, a description of forgiveness available immediately on turning, with no waiting period and no arbiter, described something the audience had no social equivalent for.
studies.didYouKnow: The second of these two ayat contains three stages in order: doing wrong, turning back after it, and believing. The Arabic then repeats the phrase after that for God's response, so within a single short sentence the word occurs twice, marking the two hinges of the sequence. Classical commentators treat the doubling as deliberate rather than as filler.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat together refuse a choice most religious writing forces. Consequence is stated plainly, without hedging, and mercy is stated immediately afterwards, also without hedging, and the Book does not tell the reader which of the two applies to them. That leaves both operative at once, which is the condition a person is actually in, and it is why the Quran so often arranges its warnings and its promises as neighbours.

crossReferences.why: States the same offer, forgiveness for whoever turns back, believes and acts rightly, then stays guided.
Puts the offer at its widest, addressed to those who exceeded all bounds against themselves.
Adds the further stage, that God exchanges bad deeds for good ones for those who turn and act.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have decided is past forgiving in yourself, and notice that the decision was yours rather than anyone else's. You do not have to feel differently about it today. Just observe that you have been holding a verdict you were never in a position to issue, and set it down for a week to see what changes.

studies.title: When The Anger Fell Silent
studies.meaning: The Arabic makes anger the subject of the sentence and says it fell silent from him. Not that he mastered it or set it aside; it stopped speaking. Commentators dwell on the image, since it describes anger as a voice that had been talking in a man and then went quiet, leaving him able to act again. Only then does he pick the tablets up. What is in their inscription is named as two things, guidance and mercy, and the recipients are described by a fronted phrase: it is their Lord that they hold in awe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the episode of the return from the mountain. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) faced provocations of a similar kind in the city, and the Quran's counsel to him throughout that period was consistently about restraint rather than about response, which is the register this ayah belongs to.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for a person ceasing to speak, with anger as its subject. Arabic thereby treats the anger as something that had been talking, and the ayah records the moment it stopped rather than the moment he chose.
From a root meaning to copy something from one place to another. The word implies a text transferred rather than composed, which matters for what the tablets are being said to contain.

A verb for reverent fear, distinct from ordinary fright. Arabic places its object before it in this ayah, which is a way of saying that it is their Lord specifically whom they hold in awe and nothing else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian culture prized both fierce anger and the ability to hold it, and had words for each. A man of forbearance was praised in poetry as highly as a man of courage, and the pairing of the two was the ideal. What everyone understood was the timing: nothing useful was decided while the anger was speaking, and a wise man was one who waited for the quiet rather than one who never felt the heat.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic sentence has no one calming anyone down. Anger is the grammatical subject, the verb is the ordinary one for falling silent, and the man is the one it falls silent from. Classical commentators note that the construction avoids saying he suppressed it, and describes instead a state passing, which is what anger actually does if nothing is said into it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are placed on either side of a pause. Before it, a scene of fury and physical action; after it, the recovery of a revelation described as guidance and mercy. Nothing is said to condemn the interval, and nothing is lost across it. The ayah's whole claim is about sequence: the same man, the same tablets, and a different capacity to hold them, separated only by the anger going quiet.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who restrain anger and pardon people, in a list of what the God-conscious are like.
Names those who forgive when they are angry, placing the forgiving inside the anger rather than after it.
Instructs repelling with what is better, so that an enemy becomes as though a close friend.

studies.applyIt: Set one rule for yourself this week: nothing decided, sent or said while the anger is still talking. Not suppressed, not resolved, just postponed until it goes quiet. Then look at the matter again. Most people find that about half of what they would have said turns out to have been the anger's words rather than their own.

studies.title: For What The Foolish Did
studies.meaning: Seventy men are chosen and a tremor takes them, and the prayer that follows is among the boldest in the Quran. It opens with a protest phrased as an observation: had You willed, You could have destroyed them earlier, and me with them. Then the question about collective liability, using for the offenders the same word a rejecting people had once thrown at a messenger in this same surah. Then a reframing, that the whole matter is a testing, and finally the request. He asks as one of them throughout, never separating himself from the people he is defending.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentators differ over what the seventy were chosen for and what the tremor was, and they record the range rather than settling it, since the Quran supplies neither. No occasion of revelation is reported. The prayer stands in the surah as the fullest example of a messenger interceding, and it is placed immediately before the answer that will become one of the Book's most quoted sentences.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning lightness and flimsiness. A rejecting people used this same word against a messenger earlier in this surah, and here a messenger uses it of his own community, with the words among us attached.
From the root describing gold put into fire to separate it from what is mixed in. Naming the whole affair a testing recasts it as a process that reveals rather than a punishment that ends.
The singular of a word used at the start of this surah for the false patrons people take beside God. The prayer returns the term to its one legitimate holder, which is the ground of the whole appeal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Collective liability was Arabian law. If a member of a clan killed, the clan paid, and if a clan sheltered a wrongdoer, the whole clan could be raided for it. A man who asked whether the many should suffer for the few was raising a question the poets and arbitrators genuinely argued about, and the answer in ordinary practice was usually yes. The prayer here is contesting something the audience lived under.
studies.didYouKnow: He never uses the word they for the people he is defending. The offenders are called the foolish among us, the punishment is asked about as will You destroy us, and the plea is forgive us and have mercy on us. Across the whole prayer, a man interceding for a community that had just made an idol keeps himself grammatically inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Intercession is shown here as identification rather than as advocacy from outside. He does not present his own record against theirs; he places himself in the same sentence as the people at fault and asks for both together. The prayer also does something rare in the Quran, which is to argue, and the argument is left in the text without being corrected, which is itself a statement about what may be brought before God.

crossReferences.why: The answer that follows immediately, widening the request far beyond what was asked for.
Shows Abraham disputing on behalf of a community, and being told to leave off the argument.
Gives another intercession that declines to plead innocence, placing the matter with God entirely.

studies.applyIt: Next time you speak up for a group you belong to that has behaved badly, notice which pronoun you use. Saying they lets you stand outside and costs you nothing. Saying we costs something and is usually the only version anyone listens to. Try it once this month, in a room where you would rather have distanced yourself.

studies.title: My Mercy Encompasses Everything
studies.meaning: The request asks for good to be written in both worlds, and the answer uses the same verb, which is how the reader knows the petition was heard on its own terms. Then two clauses that are not built the same way. Punishment is described with a will attached, striking whom He wills. Mercy is described with an extent, encompassing everything, and no limiting clause is placed on it at all. Commentators dwell on the asymmetry. What follows specifies who the written portion is for, without withdrawing the sentence that came before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this is among the most widely quoted ayat in the Quran. It arrives as the answer to a prayer of intercession made after a community had made an idol, which is to say it is spoken into the least promising circumstances the surah has described. No occasion of revelation is reported. The final clauses turn forward, and the following ayah continues the specification.

keyTerms.note: The verb of inscribing something so that it holds. The answer picks up the same verb and says I shall write it, so the reply is framed in the exact vocabulary the request used.
From a verb meaning to return by the road you came. It describes coming back rather than arriving, which fits a petition made on behalf of people who had gone somewhere else and come back.
From the root for breadth and room. The verb is in the perfect tense, so mercy is described as having already taken everything in, not as capable of doing so if occasion arises.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing was scarce and therefore weighty. A debt written down or a treaty inscribed and hung at the sanctuary had a permanence that spoken agreements did not, and people asked for things to be written when they wanted them beyond dispute. The request in this prayer uses that vocabulary, and the answer grants it in the same word, which would have registered as an undertaking rather than a reassurance.
studies.didYouKnow: The two clauses about punishment and mercy are not grammatically parallel, and the difference is the point. The first attaches a will to the reach of punishment. The second states an extent with no limiting clause at all. Classical commentators note that the Quran never phrases mercy as narrower than the thing it applies to, and this ayah is the widest instance in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A universal statement is followed by a specification, and the tradition reads the two together rather than letting either cancel the other. Mercy in this life reaches everything that exists, believer and denier, and what is written for the hereafter is described with conditions attached. This lets the ayah be quoted as widely as it is without becoming a claim that nothing matters, and it explains why hope in the Quran is always paired with a description of what to do.

crossReferences.why: The angels' prayer, which describes God as having encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge.
States that He has prescribed mercy upon Himself, using the same verb of writing.
Applies the same breadth to those who exceeded all bounds, telling them not to despair.

studies.applyIt: Take the phrase about mercy encompassing everything and apply it to one specific thing today rather than to the world in general. A situation you have written off, or a person, or yourself. Say the sentence with that one item held in mind. Universals do nothing until they are made to meet something particular, and that meeting is a two-minute exercise.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: The Burdens And The Shackles
studies.meaning: The specification continues by describing a messenger and what following him consists of. He is called unlettered, which commentators explain as being without acquired writing, as one is at birth. Then a list of what he does, and its final item is the one that carries the passage: he sets down from them their burden and the shackles that were upon them. The word for shackles shares a root with the word used earlier in this surah for the rancour removed in the Garden. Four responses are then named, and each is an act rather than an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran states that the description was found with the communities holding earlier scripture, and it presents this as a continuity rather than as a dispute; the emphasis throughout the passage is on what following amounts to rather than on any argument with anyone. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It completes the answer given to the prayer in the preceding passage.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for mother, in the sense of being as one was when born. Commentators explain it as having acquired no writing, which is why what he brought could not be traced to any book he had read.
A load that binds a person in place, from a root meaning to tie down. The word appears in the closing prayer of the longest surah, where the community asks not to be made to carry one.
Iron collars, from the same root as the word used earlier in this surah for rancour drawn out of the chest. Both name something that gets inside and then holds its bearer fast.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had very few people who could write, and the ability was a specialised trade rather than a mark of education. A man who could not write was in the ordinary position; what mattered socially was memory, and men were valued for holding poetry, genealogy and treaties in their heads. The description in this ayah would have identified a normal member of the community rather than marking anyone out as deficient.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for shackles here comes from the same root as the word used earlier in this surah for the rancour drawn out of the chests of the people of the Garden. Arabic derives both from an idea of something entering and binding. What is described as removed is therefore named with a single root twice in one surah, once inwardly and once outwardly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes following as an unburdening rather than an addition, which is the opposite of what most people expect religion to be. Loads are set down and restraints are taken off, and the four responses named afterwards are all things done rather than assented to: believing, honouring, supporting, and following a light. Attachment is described in terms of action throughout, which is how the Quran usually renders love.

crossReferences.why: Asks in prayer not to be made to carry the burden that was laid on earlier communities.
Uses the related word for rancour drawn out of the chests, the inward version of the same removal.
States the connection directly, that following him is what God's love for a person runs through.

studies.applyIt: Ask what religion currently feels like to you: something set down or something added. Both answers are common and only one matches this ayah. If yours is the second, find one obligation you have invented and are carrying that nobody actually placed on you, and put it down this week. Then notice whether anything real was lost.

studies.title: To All Of You
studies.meaning: The instruction is to say something, and the sentence is the widest address in the surah. Every messenger described in the preceding hundred ayat was sent to his own people, named as their brother, speaking their language. This one is told to say he is sent to all of you together, with the word for all placed emphatically. What follows grounds the claim in ownership of the heavens and the earth rather than in any authority of his own. Then a description of him that commentators find striking: the Prophet who himself believes in God and His words.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was addressing a city, and the scope announced here reached far past anything the Quraysh were contesting at the time. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. Its placement at the end of the surah's longest narrative is deliberate: the sequence of local missions is complete, and the last of them is described in terms none of the others were.

keyTerms.note: A word for a totality gathered rather than a sum of parts. Its position in the sentence gives it weight, and it is the term that separates this commission from every other one described in the surah.
Two verbs of the same form, one the opposite of the other. Naming both under one authority is the Quran's usual way of ruling out a division of the world between competing powers.

An unusual thing to say about a prophet. It places him among the believers rather than above them, which is consistent with the Quran's insistence that the one who delivers a message is also under it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian identity was local to its bones. A man was of a clan within a tribe within a region, and his religion, his protection and his obligations all followed those lines. Even the sanctuary at Mecca was administered by particular families with particular rights. An address to all people, with no clan, region or lineage named, had no precedent in that world and no obvious audience in it either.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah spends more than a hundred ayat on messengers each described as the brother of his own people, sent to one community, speaking its language. Then a single ayah instructs a message to be addressed to everyone. The contrast is built entirely by placement, and the Book offers no comment on the change of scope at the moment it makes it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The universal claim is grounded in ownership rather than in the messenger. Because the heavens and the earth belong to one, the message directed to all people follows, and the man delivering it is described as one of those who believe what he carries. That construction keeps the scope of the message from becoming a claim about the standing of the person announcing it, which is the shape the Quran gives to every commission in the surah.

crossReferences.why: States the same scope, that he was sent to all people as a bearer of news and a warner.
Describes the sending as a mercy to all the worlds, in one short ayah.
Shows the messenger believing in what was sent down to him, alongside the believers, as here.

studies.applyIt: Notice how local your sense of religious belonging is: your community, your language, the way things are done where you are. None of that is wrong. But find one thing this week from a Muslim community very unlike yours, a recitation, a scholar, a practice, and take it seriously for an hour. The ayah's scope is worth occasionally testing.

studies.title: A Community That Guides
studies.meaning: One short ayah, and it does something the surrounding passages do not. After a long account of a community's failures, it states that among that same people is a group who guide by the truth and who act justly by it. Nothing is qualified and nothing is taken back. The verb for acting justly comes from a root meaning to balance two things until they are equal, so guiding and weighing belong to one vocabulary. Commentators note that the Quran states this of a people it has just been describing at their worst.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent forty ayat on the calf, the tremor and the intercession, and this sentence arrives without transition. No occasion of revelation is reported. Later in the same surah the identical wording is applied to humanity in general rather than to one people, which frames this ayah as a particular case of something the Book says more widely about every group of human beings.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, so a community rather than the community. The word covers any body of people with a shared character, and its indefiniteness keeps the statement from being a claim about numbers.

The active verb, so they are described as guiding others rather than as being guided. The Quran distinguishes the two carefully, and here it credits the harder of them to a people it has just criticised.
From a root meaning to make two things equal in weight, which also gives the word for a counterweight on a pack animal. Justice in this vocabulary is an act of balancing rather than a principle held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs argued constantly about the collective character of other tribes, and satire built on it was a recognised art form. A whole people would be dismissed for the conduct of a few, and the insult would be recited for generations. Against that habit, a sentence that stops in the middle of a long criticism to name a group within the criticised people as guides would have cut directly across how the audience used language.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact wording appears twice in this surah. Here it describes a community among the people of Moses. Twenty ayat later the identical phrase, guiding by the truth and acting justly by it, is applied to those God created, without any people being named. The same sentence therefore does duty for one community and for humanity at large.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to let a long account of failure become a verdict on a people. It arrives without argument and without softening what preceded it, which is how the Quran usually handles this: it does not withdraw a criticism, it simply declines to generalise it. The pairing of guiding with justice matters too, since it makes the mark of such a community what it does for others rather than what it holds.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical wording later in this surah, applied to those God created rather than one people.
Says plainly that they are not all alike, and describes an upright community among them.
Names a moderate community among them, distinguishing it from those doing evil.

studies.applyIt: Take a group you have a settled negative opinion about and name one person in it you respect. If you cannot, that is a fact about the range of people you know rather than about the group. Either way, do not soften the criticism you hold. Just add the exception, out loud, the next time you make it.

studies.title: Each Knew Its Drinking Place
studies.meaning: Provision arrives in three forms and each comes organised. Twelve springs for twelve groups, with every group knowing which was theirs, so the water carries an allocation rather than an opportunity to fight. Then shade, then food sent down. The verb used here for the water emerging means a first seeping, while the parallel account in another surah uses one meaning a full bursting, and classical commentators read the two as consecutive stages of one thing. The closing line places the damage entirely on the side of the people.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to an audience for whom every element in this description was a live concern: water rights, shade, and food arriving without being grown. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The passage stands between two general statements about the community, and it works as an inventory of what had been supplied, given just before the account of what was done with it resumes.

keyTerms.note: A verb for water first breaking through, gently. Another surah describes the same event with a verb meaning to burst open fully, and commentators read the two as the beginning and the completion of one event.
A noun of place from the verb to drink. The ayah says each group knew theirs, so what is described includes an allocation, which is the part that keeps twelve groups from fighting over water.
From the root for shade, which in Arabic belongs to the vocabulary of relief rather than of darkness. Shade in a desert is not an absence of light but the condition that makes daytime survivable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the sharpest question in Arabian life, and wells were allocated by turns everyone knew and disputed anyway. Fights broke out over a day's precedence. Shade was managed too, since a tribe camped where a rock or a stand of palms gave it, and travellers rested through the worst hours or died. The three provisions listed here are, in that order, what a desert journey actually required.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this episode in two surahs and changes one verb. Here the springs seep forth; in the other account they burst open. Classical commentators note that the two verbs describe different moments of a single event, the first trickle and the full flow, and read them as complementary rather than as versions to be chosen between.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The provision described has structure built into it, which is easy to read past. Twelve springs matched to twelve groups is not more water than one spring would be; it is water arranged so that receiving it does not become an occasion for conflict. The closing formula then places everything that followed on the human side, in a construction saying the wrong done reached nobody except the people doing it.

crossReferences.why: The parallel account, using the other verb for the springs and listing the same three provisions.
Names the same food and warns against transgressing in what had been provided.
Describes the striking of the sea with the staff, the other occasion on which the staff opens water.

studies.applyIt: Look at something you share with other people and ask whether the arrangement is actually clear: whose turn, whose portion, who decides. Most friction over shared things is about allocation rather than scarcity. Fix one such arrangement this week by naming it aloud instead of assuming it. The ayah presents the allocation as part of the gift.

studies.title: Enter The Gate Bowing
studies.meaning: Four instructions and a promise. Settle here, eat freely, say one particular word, and enter the gate lowered. The word they are told to say means the setting down of a load, so it is a request for a burden to be lifted rather than a formula of any other kind. Commentators differ over the posture, some reading full prostration and others a bowing of the head, since a gate cannot easily be entered face down. The promise attached is doubled: forgiveness, and then an increase for those who do well.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This instruction appears in two surahs, and the two versions give the same four elements with the word and the gate in opposite order. Classical commentators note the variation without treating it as a discrepancy. No occasion of revelation is reported. What followed is given in the next ayah, where the word they were told to say is exchanged for a different one.

keyTerms.gloss: a setting down of the load
keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to unload an animal or put a burden on the ground. Commentators explain it as asking for the weight of wrongdoing to be taken off, which is how one word can carry a whole request.
A plural participle describing their bearing as they enter. Commentators read it as full prostration or as bowing the head, noting that a gateway makes the first difficult, and they record both.
From a root joining goodness with beauty, so the word means doing a thing finely rather than merely correctly. The increase promised is attached to that quality rather than to the entering itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Entering a town was a formal act with a bearing attached. A defeated party came in bareheaded and on foot; an honoured guest rode. Anyone watching a gate could read a person's standing from how they came through it, and there were words spoken at thresholds too, asking leave or invoking protection. The instruction here uses that whole grammar, pairing a word with a posture at the exact point where both were read.
studies.didYouKnow: This instruction appears twice in the Quran with its two central clauses in opposite order. One surah gives the gate first and then the word; this one gives the word first and then the gate. Everything else is preserved, which is characteristic of how the Book repeats a passage with a single deliberate variation and no comment on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage pairs speech with posture and treats neither as sufficient alone. A word is given to say and a bearing to adopt, and the promise attaches to both together, which is the Quran's usual way of describing a turning back: something said and something done with the body at the same time. The doubled promise then separates being forgiven from being increased, so pardon is not the ceiling of what is offered.

crossReferences.why: The same instruction with the gate and the word given in the opposite order.
Reports what followed, the word replaced by a different one from the one they were given.
Pairs a movement with a request for forgiveness in the same way, in the pilgrimage passages.

studies.applyIt: Think of an apology you owe that you have been planning to make in writing. Consider doing it in person instead, or at least by voice. The instruction here attaches a posture to a word because the two together cost something the word alone does not, and that difference in cost is most of what makes an apology land.

studies.title: A Word Other Than
studies.meaning: One word was given to say and a different one was said instead, and the ayah does not report which. It reports only that a substitution took place. Commentators note the restriction built into the sentence: it names the wrongdoers among them rather than the community, and the consequence is directed at the same restricted group. What follows arrives from the sky and is called by a word meaning something repellent, the same term used earlier in this surah for the afflictions sent on Egypt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this episode twice, and both tellings keep the limitation to those who did wrong, one by repeating the phrase and this one by adding a word meaning among them. No occasion of revelation is reported. It follows immediately on the instruction of the preceding ayah, so the reader has just been told what was asked for before being told what was done with it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for putting one thing in another's place, so the position was kept and the content swapped. Nothing was refused outright, which is what makes the act a substitution rather than a rejection.

A partitive, restricting the subject to a portion of the community. The Quran keeps the restriction in both places where it tells this, and the consequence in the same ayah is directed only at that portion.
A word for something repellent, used earlier in this surah for what was sent upon Egypt. It names the quality of what arrives rather than its form, which is why the Quran gives no description of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Formulas mattered in a society without documents. The exact wording of an oath, a truce or a marriage was what made it binding, and altering a syllable could void the whole arrangement or start a feud. Witnesses were kept precisely to remember the words. An audience trained to hold a formula exactly would have understood at once why replacing one word with another counted as an act rather than a slip.
studies.didYouKnow: The word chosen to be said was a request for a burden to be set down, one syllable long. What the Quran records is not that it was refused but that something else was put in its place. Both tellings in the Book withhold the substituted word entirely, so the reader is never told what was actually said, only that the exchange happened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a small alteration in speech as a serious matter, because the words in question were the whole of what was asked. Where a request has been reduced to one thing, changing that thing is not a partial compliance but a complete substitution. The care the ayah takes in restricting the subject is equally deliberate, since it keeps a community's failure attached to the people who committed it.

crossReferences.why: The other telling, which keeps the same restriction to the wrongdoers by repeating the phrase.
The instruction that was given, including the word to say and the posture to enter with.
Describes displacing words from their places, with speech twisted by tongues in another setting.

studies.applyIt: Notice the small substitutions in your own speech this week: I will try instead of I will, someone should instead of I should, we for I when something went wrong. Each is a word put in another's place and each changes what was actually said. Catch one and put the original word back.

studies.title: The Town By The Sea
studies.meaning: The test is described with unusual precision. On the day of restraint the fish came, surfacing where everyone could see them, and on other days they did not. Commentators note the calibration: the abundance arrived exactly when it could not be taken, so the difficulty was not scarcity but the sight of plenty placed just out of reach. The verb for their transgressing means going beyond a limit rather than doing something in itself harmful, and the closing clause calls the whole arrangement a testing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the ayah opens by telling the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to ask them about it, so the episode was already known to the people being addressed. The Quran never names the town. Classical commentators offer several coastal identifications and record them as reports rather than as settled fact, which is the same restraint the Book shows elsewhere about details it withholds.

keyTerms.note: A phrase meaning right on the shore rather than merely coastal. The town's whole livelihood is established in three words, which is why nothing further needs saying about why fish mattered so much.

A rare plural describing the fish raising themselves at the water's surface. Commentators explain it as coming visibly and within reach, which is the detail that makes the restraint difficult rather than merely inconvenient.

From a root meaning to run past a boundary, used of an animal breaking out of enclosed ground. It names crossing a line rather than any harm in the act itself, which is what a limit-based test consists of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had its own version of this. During the sacred months raiding stopped, and caravans that would have been irresistible at any other time of year passed unmolested within sight of men who could easily have taken them. Everyone knew what it was to watch something valuable go by under a restriction they had accepted. The whole peninsular economy depended on that restraint holding four months a year.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives this episode in two surahs and names the town in neither. Classical commentators offer several identifications along the Red Sea and further north, and present them as reports. The Book withholds the name in the same way it withholds the tree in the Garden and the identity of the man in the parable a few ayat later.
