studies.theologicalSignificance: The test described is designed rather than incidental, and the design is what the ayah makes visible. Abundance was placed precisely where it could not be taken, which means the difficulty was arranged for the purpose. That says something specific about how the Quran understands testing: not as hardship allowed to happen, but as a setting of circumstances that reveals what a limit is actually worth to the person keeping it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same episode in one short ayah, with the outcome and none of the circumstances.
Describes another test involving game coming within easy reach, with a restraint attached.
States the principle, that what is on the earth was made an ornament in order to test conduct.

studies.applyIt: Think of the limit you keep that is hardest, and notice when it is hardest. It is almost never when the thing is unavailable. It is when it is right there, easy, and nobody would know. That moment is the whole test, and recognising it as the test rather than as bad luck changes how it feels to be standing in it.

studies.title: Why Do You Counsel Them
studies.meaning: A group inside the town asks the others why they bother, and the question is not cynical. It assumes the outcome is already settled, so speaking looks like wasted breath. The answer gives two reasons and they are of different orders. The first is a discharge before their Lord, which does not depend on any result at all. The second is introduced by the particle of hope: perhaps they will guard themselves. Commentators note that the reason which depends on success is placed second and stated as a possibility.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The believers in the city were speaking to people who had been refusing for years, and the question of whether to keep speaking was a live one for them. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. In the surah it comes just before the outcome, so the reader hears the argument about whether to speak before learning what happened to each of the parties having it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for speech meant to soften a hearer and move them to change. It names counsel aimed at the heart rather than argument aimed at the mind, which is why the question about futility bites.
A noun for what clears a person of responsibility. The first reason given is therefore about the speakers rather than the hearers, and it holds whether or not anything is achieved.
The particle of hope, which stops the clause short of expectation. Placing it on the second reason keeps the whole answer honest, since the speakers do not claim to think it likely.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public counsel in a small town was costly and awkward. Everyone knew everyone, and telling a neighbour he was wrong meant living beside him afterwards. Arabs had a word of praise for the man who did it anyway and a whole vocabulary of resentment for how it was received. The question asked here, whether it is worth the trouble when nothing will change, is one that community had certainly asked before.
studies.didYouKnow: The answer does not defend the counselling by claiming it will work. It gives a reason that holds regardless of outcome, and only then adds the hope of an outcome, marked with a particle that means it may be so. Classical commentators dwell on the order, since it grounds the whole activity in something the speaker controls.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates responsibility from effectiveness, which is a distinction that keeps people speaking long after they have stopped expecting results. It also treats the objection seriously rather than dismissing it, since the objectors are not accused of anything in the ayah. What is being modelled is a way of continuing that neither requires optimism nor collapses into futility, and the two reasons together are what make that possible.

crossReferences.why: Instructs continuing to remind, on the ground that reminding benefits the believers.
Limits the messenger's role to reminding, saying he is not set over them as a controller.
Has a messenger say he intends only reform as far as he is able, with success resting elsewhere.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you have stopped saying because it never lands. You may be right that it will not land. Say it once more anyway, briefly and without pressure, and then let it go. This ayah offers a reason for speaking that does not depend on being heard, which is the only reason that survives long relationships.

studies.title: Those Who Forbade The Wrong
studies.meaning: Two outcomes are reported where three groups have been described. The people who overstepped are seized, and the people who forbade the wrong are delivered. The group who had asked why anyone bothered is not mentioned at either end. This silence is one of the oldest discussions in the commentary tradition, and the reports preserve a long uncertainty about them before a conclusion was reached. The transformation announced in the second ayah is read by most classical authorities as literal and by some as a likeness of character.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ibn Abbas is reported to have spent a long time uncertain about the fate of the third group before concluding that they were saved, and the report is preserved in the major commentaries as an account of how the question was worked through rather than as a ruling handed down. No occasion of revelation is attached to these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The deliverance is attached to this description rather than to abstaining. Those saved are named by what they said to others, not by what they refrained from doing themselves, which the commentators note carefully.

A rare adjectival form from the root for hardship and distress. Its unusual shape gives the word an emphasis that the ordinary form would not carry, which is why translations reach for terms like dire.
From a verb used of shooing an animal away. It describes being repelled and made small, and it appears elsewhere in the Quran of a gaze that returns humbled after searching for a flaw.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Silence was the ordinary strategy in a small community. A man who neither joined a wrong nor objected to it kept his standing with everyone, and Arabian society had no mechanism that required him to choose. The question of whether such a person shares in what happens to a town was therefore not abstract. It was the position most people occupied most of the time, and everyone knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: Three groups are described in these ayat and only two outcomes are given. The commentary tradition preserves a long-running uncertainty about the group who had asked why anyone was bothering, and the reports show the question being weighed for years before a view settled. The Quran itself simply leaves them out of the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is attached to speaking rather than to abstaining, which raises the bar in an uncomfortable direction. The passage does not say the rescued had kept the limit, though presumably they had; it says they forbade the wrong. That makes objection itself a form of participation in a community's fate, and it explains why the tradition treated the missing third group as a genuinely open question rather than an obvious one.

crossReferences.why: Gives the exchange between the two groups that these ayat then resolve, or partly resolve.
Names the failure to forbid wrongdoing among one another as what a curse fell upon.
Tells the same outcome briefly and calls it an example for what lay before it and after it.

studies.applyIt: Recall a situation where you neither joined in nor objected. Most of us are in one now. You do not have to make a scene. Say the smallest true thing to one person: I am not comfortable with this. It costs about four seconds, and it moves you out of the group this passage declines to mention.

studies.title: Swift And Yet Forgiving
studies.meaning: The announcement is made with a verb meaning to proclaim something so it is known. What is announced concerns the community the surah has been describing, and the phrase used for what will come against them is word for word the phrase used earlier in this same surah for what Egypt had done to them. Then the ayah closes with two descriptions of God that pull in opposite directions: swift in requital, and forgiving, merciful. Commentators read the pairing as deliberate, and the following ayah immediately distinguishes the righteous among them from the rest.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the close of a long passage about one community's history. The Quran regularly attaches this pair of divine descriptions to its severest statements, and the same two clauses appear together at the end of another surah in exactly this order. No occasion of revelation is reported. What follows in the next ayah is a differentiation that classical commentators always read together with this one.

keyTerms.note: From the root for giving ear, in a form meaning to proclaim so that it cannot be missed. The verb concerns publication rather than decision, so what is described is a declaration already made.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for what Egypt did to them, taken from herding and pricing. The Book applies one expression to the oppression suffered and to what is announced here.
Requital here is from a root meaning to follow on the heel, so it names what comes after an act rather than a penalty imposed on it. Swiftness describes the closeness of the following, not haste.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Proclamation was how anything became binding. A herald stood at a gathering, the terms were called out, and from that moment nobody could claim not to have known. Treaties, outlawries and the opening of a market all worked this way. The verb used at the start of this ayah belongs to that setting, and it describes something put on the public record rather than a decision reached in private.
studies.didYouKnow: The two divine descriptions that close this ayah appear together, in the same order and almost the same words, at the end of another surah entirely. The Quran habitually places forgiveness and mercy immediately after its statements about requital, and classical commentators treat the pairing as a fixed feature rather than as a softening added afterwards.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah is read in the tradition alongside the sentence that follows it, which states plainly that among them are the righteous and among them are others. Neither statement is allowed to swallow the other. And the closing pair keeps the passage from being a description of a settled fate, since requital and forgiveness are named as belonging to the same one, in the same breath, with nothing said about which any individual will meet.

crossReferences.why: The next ayah, which distinguishes the righteous among them from the rest and names both.
Closes with the identical pair of descriptions, swift in requital and yet forgiving and merciful.
States earlier in this surah that among this same people is a community that guides by truth.

studies.applyIt: When you read a severe passage, make a habit of reading the clause that follows it before you decide what it means. This ayah ends by naming mercy and the next one names the righteous among the people just described. Whole readings have been built by stopping one sentence early, and the habit of not stopping is cheap to acquire.

studies.title: Some Of Them Righteous
studies.meaning: The dividing is named first, and the verb is the same one used earlier in this surah for the twelve tribes, so the same word does duty for an ordering and a scattering. Then the sentence the whole passage turns on: among them are the righteous and among them are those short of that. Nothing is quantified. Then the testing, and it comes in both directions, with good things and with bad, which rules out reading either as a verdict. The stated purpose is a returning, introduced by the particle of hope.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this ayah is where the surah's long account of one community lands. Classical commentators consistently read it alongside the severe statement immediately before it, since it is the sentence that prevents the preceding passage from becoming a description of a whole people. No occasion of revelation is reported for it, and the surah moves on to a general statement about inheritors in the next ayah.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used earlier in this surah for dividing them into twelve tribes. One word covers an orderly arrangement in one place and a scattering across the earth in the other, without changing form.

A phrase meaning below or other than the thing just named. It declines to specify what the second group is, describing them only by their distance from the first, which is a deliberately unfinished description.
Both are named as instruments of testing, in that order. Since the two are given the same role, neither can be read as a report on the standing of whoever receives it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs generalised about peoples constantly, and satire built on collective character was a recognised art. A whole tribe would be summed up in a line of verse that stuck for generations, and everyone knew the reputations. Against a background where that was the normal way of speaking about others, a sentence that stops to say some of them are righteous and some are not would have registered as a refusal of the ordinary idiom.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for scattering them here is the identical verb used a few ayat earlier for dividing them into twelve tribes, where it describes an orderly arrangement with water allocated to each group. The Quran uses one word for both, so the same act of dividing appears once as provision and once as dispersal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Testing is described as running in both directions, and that is the ayah's most portable claim. If good fortune and misfortune are both instruments, then neither can be used to read anyone's standing, including one's own. The stated purpose is a returning rather than a punishment, and the differentiation at the centre of the ayah keeps the whole preceding passage from being turned into a statement about a people as such.

crossReferences.why: Names a community among them that guides by truth, in the same surah and the same terms.
States plainly that they are not all alike, describing an upright group reciting through the night.
Gives the same principle generally, that people are tested with evil and with good as a trial.

studies.applyIt: Take the last general statement you made about a group of people and add the qualification this ayah adds. Some of them, and some of them not. It does not require you to change your assessment of anything you actually observed. It requires you to stop applying it to people you have not met, which is a smaller ask than it sounds.

studies.title: We Will Be Forgiven
studies.meaning: The word for the generation that followed is the form Arabic reserves for an unworthy successor, distinguished by a single vowel from a nearly identical word used for a worthy one. They inherited a Book and took the passing goods of this lower world, and then said the sentence the ayah is built around: we will be forgiven. What follows is the sharpest observation. If the like comes again, they take it again. The presumption is not a response to a lapse but a standing arrangement that makes the next one available.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage is about people who had a scripture, studied it, and used a doctrine drawn from it to keep doing what it addressed. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It sits at the point where the surah turns from one community's history to a general statement, and it is followed immediately by a description of those who hold the Book firmly, so both possibilities are named.

keyTerms.note: Arabic distinguishes two nearly identical nouns from this root by one vowel, one used for a worthy successor and one for an unworthy one. This ayah uses the second, so the assessment is made in the noun itself.
A word for what appears briefly and moves on, used in Arabic for anything incidental rather than substantial. The phrase attaches it to this lower world, so the transience is named twice over.
An intensive form from the root for tying tightly. It names an undertaking made firm rather than a promise given, and the ayah says it was taken upon them rather than offered to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs had their own version of a doctrine that made things easier. The sanctuary's custodians granted concessions to their own clans, and various customs allowed a man to postpone or exchange an obligation he found inconvenient while keeping the appearance of observing it. Everyone recognised the manoeuvre. What the ayah describes is not a foreign failing but a very familiar one, done with a scripture instead of a custom.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah notes that they studied what was in the Book, using the ordinary verb for reading something repeatedly until it is learned. Knowledge is therefore not what was missing. Classical commentators dwell on this clause, since it removes the usual explanation for such conduct and leaves only the presumption named in the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a specific misuse of the doctrine of forgiveness, which is using it in advance. Turning back after a wrong is the whole subject of the ayat a few pages earlier; here the same expectation is moved to the front and becomes a licence. The Quran does not respond by withdrawing forgiveness. It responds by pointing out that the second taking has already been decided on, which is what a covenant was supposed to prevent.

crossReferences.why: Distinguishes turning back soon after a wrong from the turning offered when death arrives.
The next ayah, describing those who hold fast to the Book, as the immediate counterpart.
Warns against being deceived about God by the great deceiver, and against worldly life deceiving you.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the moment you decide in advance that something will be all right. Not afterwards, when regret is real, but before, while the decision is still being made. That sentence is doing work, and it is worth catching once. You do not need to conclude anything about forgiveness. Just notice what the thought was for.

studies.title: Those Who Hold It Firmly
studies.meaning: The counterpart is given in one sentence. Those who hold the Book firmly, using an intensive verb for gripping, and who establish the prayer, and the reward promised is attached to a word meaning those who put things right. Then the mountain, raised over them like an awning. The word chosen for that canopy comes from the root for shade, so the thing suspended above them in threat is named with the vocabulary of shelter. The instruction given underneath it is the same one given to Moses with the tablets.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The raising of the mountain is mentioned several times in the Quran and always in a few words, without any account of how long it lasted or how it ended. Classical commentators do not elaborate beyond the text. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The pairing here is deliberate: the generation who presumed on forgiveness is described, and then those who did the opposite.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb for grasping, so the holding is described as continuous and effortful. It stands directly against the taking described in the preceding ayah, which used a verb of casual acquisition.
A rare verb for pulling something up forcefully from where it sits. The Quran uses it only here, and its violence is part of what makes the following image so strange.
From the root for shade, and the ordinary word for something spread overhead to shelter people. Naming the suspended mountain with it puts the vocabulary of protection on an object about to fall.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An awning was the most welcome object in Arabian life. A cloth stretched over poles at a market, the shade side of a tent, a rock ledge at noon: these were where business was done and where a traveller survived the middle of the day. To be under a canopy was to be safe. The ayah takes that association and puts a mountain in the position the cloth would occupy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the mountain's shape overhead is built on the root for shade, which in Arabic is the vocabulary of relief and hospitality rather than of darkness or menace. The Quran therefore describes a thing they expected to fall on them using the same noun a family would use for the awning they ate their meal beneath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat set an image against a practice. The instruction given under the mountain is to hold what was given with strength and to remember what is in it, which is exactly what the previous ayah's generation had failed to do while studying it. And the reward named is for those who put things right, so the holding described is not private possession of a text but work done with it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same raising of the mountain and the same instruction to hold firmly and remember.
Contains the identical instruction given with the tablets, to take what was given with strength.
Mentions the mountain raised over them again, alongside other undertakings taken from them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you know from your religion and have never actually put to work. Not a new practice, something you already hold. Use it once this week on a real decision, and see what it does. The ayah joins holding to putting right, and a conviction that has never been applied to anything is not yet being held.

studies.title: Am I Not Your Lord
studies.meaning: Descendants are brought out and made to bear witness about themselves, and a single question is put. Classical commentators divide over what is being described: an actual assembly of all human beings before their entry into the world, or the disposition placed in every person at their making, and the tradition preserves both readings. The answer given is one Arabic particle used only to contradict a negative, so it does not mean agreement but denial of the denial. The stated purpose is to close off one excuse.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah has been among the most discussed in the Quran since the earliest period, and the commentators record their difference without either side treating the other as outside the mainstream. No occasion of revelation is reported. It arrives at the point where the surah turns from the histories of particular communities to a statement about every human being, and the ayat following continue that widening.

keyTerms.note: A particle Arabic uses only to contradict a negative question. Had they answered with the ordinary word for yes, grammarians note, it would have agreed with the negation rather than denying it.
The verb for causing someone to bear witness, with themselves as the object of the testimony. They are not asked to observe something else but to give evidence about their own condition.
The excuse ruled out is not ignorance but heedlessness, which is the state of having something available and not attending to it. The Quran uses this word throughout the surah for the same condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the backbone of Arabian dispute. Nothing was written, so an agreement was made binding by witnesses who could be produced years later, and the strongest position in any quarrel was to have been present when the words were said. A man who could say I was there and I heard it settled matters. The ayah puts every human being in that position with respect to themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The single word used to answer the question is a particle with no English equivalent. Arabic distinguishes between agreeing with a negative question and denying it, and this word does only the second. Grammarians cite this ayah as the standard example, since answering with the ordinary word for yes would have meant conceding that He is not their Lord.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Whichever reading of the event is taken, the passage locates something prior to argument in every human being. The excuse that is closed off is not the absence of information but the failure to attend to what was already there, which shifts the whole question from proof to attention. It also makes the testimony self-given, so nobody is being held to a covenant somebody else entered on their behalf.

crossReferences.why: Describes an original disposition on which people were made, which many read alongside this.
The next ayah, which closes off the second excuse, that one's forebears associated others with God.
Recalls a covenant taken with the children of Adam, in the other place they are addressed that way.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself when you last simply attended to being alive, without a task attached. Ten seconds at a window counts. The excuse this ayah closes off is inattention rather than ignorance, which means the remedy is not more information. It is a few minutes of the sort of noticing that nothing in an ordinary day requires of you.

studies.title: What Our Fathers Did
studies.meaning: A second excuse is closed and it is the one the surah has heard several times already: our forebears associated others with God, and we merely came after them. The plea that follows is almost word for word the plea a prophet made earlier in this surah on behalf of his own people, and the difference is instructive. That one said the foolish among us and asked; this one says the falsifiers and pleads descent. The closing ayah names what all of this is for, and the purpose given is a returning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this was the standing Quraysh defence. Their religion came with their lineage and could not be examined without insulting the men who had handed it down, which is why the Quran addresses the argument repeatedly and from several angles. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. They complete the widening begun in the preceding ayah, which moved from particular communities to every human being.

keyTerms.note: From the root for what has no substance behind it. Calling the forebears by this name inside the excuse is what makes the plea awkward, since it concedes the point while asking not to be held to it.
The same word used in the preceding ayah for the descendants brought out to testify. The excuse uses the very term the testimony was taken from, which is why it cannot succeed on its own ground.

From the root for a joint between bones and for separating things at their natural divisions. Signs articulated this way are given piece by piece, which is what makes each one a separate occasion to reconsider.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a man could not disown his ancestors' religion without disowning them, and the poets treated that as the deepest disgrace available. Genealogy was recited at every gathering and a father's name was carried for life. The excuse in this ayah is therefore not laziness; it names a real cost. What the Quran refuses is the conclusion that the cost removes the question rather than making it expensive.
studies.didYouKnow: The plea here is nearly identical in wording to one made earlier in this surah by a prophet interceding for his community after they made a calf. That one was answered with the widest statement of mercy in the Book. This one is ruled out in advance. The difference in the Arabic is which pronoun the speaker uses about the offenders.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two excuses are closed in two ayat, and between them they cover most of what people actually say. The first was that nobody told us; the second is that we were handed this. Neither is called false as a description of circumstances. What is denied is that either one transfers the answer, which leaves every person holding a question they did not choose to be asked and cannot pass on.

crossReferences.why: The prophet's plea this excuse echoes, made with himself included among the people at fault.
Puts the same appeal to forebears and asks what if they understood nothing and were unguided.
Records the argument at length, that they found their fathers on a way and are following their traces.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you believe mainly because it came with your family. It may well be true. Spend twenty minutes finding out why it is held, from someone who can explain rather than merely assert. You are not testing your parents. You are converting an inheritance into something you can actually answer for.

studies.title: He Slipped Out Of Them
studies.meaning: The instruction is to recite an account, and the man in it is not named. What he was given is stated plainly: Our signs. The verb describing what he did with them is the one used of a snake leaving its skin and of a month slipping away, so the signs are pictured as something he was inside and came out of. Then a reversal of the usual order. Rather than a person pursuing an adversary, the adversary follows him, which commentators read as the consequence of the stripping rather than its cause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentators offer several identifications for the man, including figures from Israelite tradition and from Arabia itself, and they record these as reports without settling on one. The Quran withholds the name deliberately, as it withholds the town by the sea and the tree in the Garden. No occasion of revelation is reported, and the following ayah supplies the likeness that explains him.

keyTerms.gloss: so he slipped out of them
keyTerms.note: The verb for a skin being stripped from a body and for a snake leaving its own. The Quran also uses it of the sacred months passing away, so it covers both a shedding and a season sliding by.
The order is reversed from what one might expect. The adversary follows the man rather than the man following him, which places the departure first and the pursuit as what it made possible.
From the root used in this surah for the vow made in the Garden, where the same word described being led off course. The man ends in the category the whole surah opened by describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Snakes were common, and their shed skins were a familiar sight in rocky country: an intact shape of an animal that was no longer in it. The image was proverbial, and Arabs used the word for anything that had left the form it once filled. Applied to a man and his knowledge, it says that what he knew is still there in outline and he is not inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here appears elsewhere in the Quran for the passing away of the sacred months, so the same word covers a skin shed and a season slipping by. Both senses are gradual. Nothing in the vocabulary suggests a sudden break, which is part of why classical commentators describe the man's condition as a departure rather than a decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge is presented as something a person can be inside and can leave, which makes it a location rather than a possession. That is an uncomfortable claim, since it means having been given the signs is not a state anyone occupies permanently. The reversal in the second half is equally exact: the pursuit follows the departure, so what is described is not a person overcome but a person who stepped out of cover.

crossReferences.why: The next ayah, which gives the likeness explaining what he did and why he could not be raised.
Uses the same verb for the sacred months slipping away, showing its ordinary sense of gradual passing.
Gives a matching image of carrying a book without bearing it, using an animal loaded with volumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you once knew well and have quietly stopped living inside: a practice you understood, a subject you cared about, a way you used to treat people. Nothing dramatic happened; you simply came out of it. Step back in for one hour this week. Skins are easier to re-enter than the image suggests.

studies.title: It Pants Either Way
studies.meaning: The raising was available and did not happen, and the reason is given in a verb built from the root for permanence. He inclined to the earth as though he would stay in it forever. Then the desire he followed, named with a word whose root means falling. The likeness that follows is exact. A dog pants when driven and pants when left alone, so the panting comes from inside rather than from the circumstance, and commentators dwell on this: what is described is not a response to pressure but a condition that pressure does not alter.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this likeness at the end of a long surah about communities who were shown things and did not change, and it applies the picture to that whole pattern rather than to one man. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It closes with an instruction to narrate the account so that people may think, which is the surah handing its material to the reader.

keyTerms.note: Built from the root for permanence and eternal remaining. The verb describes leaning towards something as though intending never to leave it, which is why the object of the leaning being the earth is the whole point.

From a root meaning to fall or descend. Arabic names desire with the vocabulary of falling, so the word already contains a direction, and the Quran uses it consistently for wanting that pulls downward.

The specific verb for a dog's open-mouthed breathing. Commentators note that other animals pant only when driven or exhausted, so naming an animal that pants either way is what makes the likeness work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dogs in Arabia were working animals, kept for herding and hunting rather than for company, and everyone had watched them. The detail the likeness turns on is one any child in that world would have noticed without being told: the dog runs and pants, then lies in the shade and pants. Nothing in the animal's state tracks what is happening to it, which is exactly the point being made.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison works on a fact of animal behaviour rather than on a moral about dogs. Classical commentators are explicit about this: the likeness turns on the panting being unconditioned, present under exertion and at rest alike, so it names a restlessness that circumstances neither cause nor relieve. Change the animal and the image stops working.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a state in which nothing that happens makes any difference, which is the most serious condition the surah has named. Signs were given and left; a raising was possible and refused; and the likeness explains why more evidence would change nothing, since the restlessness described is not produced by anything outside. The closing instruction is nonetheless to keep telling the account, which leaves the door where the surah has kept it throughout.

crossReferences.why: The preceding ayah, which gives the man this likeness explains and the signs he came out of.
Describes one who takes his own desire as his god, with hearing and heart sealed over.
Asks about the same figure and compares such people to cattle, or further astray than cattle.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your restlessness actually tracks your circumstances. Test it on a good day rather than a bad one. If the same background hum is there when nothing is wrong, the hum is not about the situation and no change in the situation will settle it. That is worth knowing before you rearrange anything.

studies.title: An Evil Likeness
studies.meaning: The first ayah passes a verdict on the picture just given and then adds a clause that relocates the damage: it was their own selves they were wronging. Nothing is said about harm done to anyone else. The second ayah states the matter as a pair of clauses, and the Arabic is careful. Whom God guides, he is the guided one, with the definite article, so guidance is not merely conferred but constitutes the person. Whom He leaves to stray, those are the losers, and the word is again commercial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage about the man who came out of the signs and the likeness of the dog. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. They function as the summary of everything the surah has been showing across its narratives, which is why the language turns from story to statement at exactly this point, just before the surah's final section begins.

keyTerms.note: A construction of blame in Arabic, used to condemn something by naming its category. The verdict falls on the likeness rather than on individuals, which keeps the assessment attached to a pattern of conduct.
The object is placed before its verb, which in Arabic gives it emphasis. The sentence therefore says it was themselves, and nobody else, that they were wronging all along.
Definite, so not a guided person but the guided one. The construction makes guidance identify the person rather than describe a state they happen to be in at a given moment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Likenesses were how Arabs argued. A proverb or a comparison settled a dispute more effectively than reasoning did, and a well-made image entered the language and was quoted for generations. Poets competed to produce them. To close a comparison by calling it an evil likeness was to pass judgement in the genre the audience took most seriously, using their own critical vocabulary against the thing described.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran places the word for their own selves before its verb in the first of these ayat, a word order Arabic uses for emphasis. The effect is to insist on the object: the wrongdoing had a target, and the target was the people doing it. The construction recurs across the Book wherever this point is made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat put a hard pairing side by side without softening either half. Guidance is credited entirely upward, and loss is described as self-inflicted, which is the same asymmetry the surah used much earlier for a rescue and a ruin. Holding both at once is uncomfortable and the Quran does not resolve it here, leaving a reader with responsibility for the loss and no claim on the guidance.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that God does not wrong people at all, but that people wrong themselves.
Says whoever is guided is guided for his own soul, and whoever strays does so against it.
Uses the same pair of clauses about guiding and leaving to stray, in almost identical wording.

studies.applyIt: Take one habit you know is not good for you and describe its cost only in terms of yourself. Not what it does to your family, not what people think. Just the cost to you. Most people find this harder than the other version and more accurate, and it removes the negotiation about whether anyone else really minds.

studies.title: Hearts That Do Not Understand
studies.meaning: Three faculties are listed and each is described as present and unused. They have hearts they do not understand with, eyes they do not see with, ears they do not hear with. The grammar is careful: nothing is missing. What is denied is the use of an instrument that is there. Then the comparison, and it is made twice, first likening them to grazing animals and then correcting itself to say they are further off the road. The closing word is the surah's recurring one for inattention.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran repeatedly describes refusal as a failure of reception rather than of information, and this is the fullest statement of that in the surah. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes near the end of the chapter, after every kind of sign has been described being given and refused, and it supplies the explanation the narratives had implied.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scattering seed and for bringing creatures out in numbers. It names propagation rather than an act of making, which is why the ayah reads as a description of a population rather than of individuals.

From a root meaning to grasp the inner sense of a thing rather than merely to know it. The heart is named as the organ of that grasping, which is the Quran's steady position on where understanding happens.
The word for herd animals kept for milk and meat, not for wild beasts. The comparison names creatures that eat, move and do not consider, which is the specific quality the likeness is reaching for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock were the measure of everything in Arabia, and their behaviour was watched closely all day long. A herd follows grass, drinks, lies down and follows grass again, and it does this whether the season is good or the tribe is at war. Nobody thought of them as stupid. They were thought of as creatures fully occupied by what was in front of them, which is exactly what the comparison uses.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison is made and then immediately revised. They are like grazing animals, and then a particle of correction says rather, they are further astray. Arabic uses that word to withdraw a statement and replace it with a stronger one, so the ayah records its own comparison being found insufficient in the middle of the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faculties are described as given for a purpose and measured by whether the purpose is served. That makes possession of an instrument irrelevant on its own, and it explains the whole surah's account of signs that were seen and changed nothing. The correction added to the comparison matters too: an animal fully occupied by what is in front of it is doing what it was made for, and a human being doing the same is not.

crossReferences.why: States the same point directly, that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.
Makes the same comparison to cattle and the same correction, that they are further astray.
Later in this surah, the mirror image: objects that lack the faculties these people possess.

studies.applyIt: Pick one faculty and use it properly for ten minutes today. Look at something without photographing it. Listen to someone without preparing an answer. Read a page without checking anything. The ayah's complaint is not about equipment, and the remedy is at exactly this scale, which is why it is available on a Tuesday.

studies.title: Call Him By His Names
studies.meaning: Two statements with an instruction between them. The names belong to God, they are described as the most beautiful, and the response asked for is to use them in calling on Him. Early scholars note that the verse neither lists them nor fixes their number. Then a second instruction, to leave alone those who distort the names. That is unusually restrained. No argument is prescribed, only withdrawal, with the outcome left where it belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Early scholars connect the verse with the practice of deriving names for local gods from the divine name itself. That is what the word for distortion is taken to describe. The surah has spent much of its length on invented religion. This verse addresses the same problem at the level of vocabulary rather than at the level of ritual.

keyTerms.note: A superlative in the feminine, from a root for beauty and for what is good. It qualifies the names as a set, so the beauty is claimed for the whole vocabulary rather than for any single term in it.
The verb covers both calling someone by a name and calling on them for help. The verse uses both senses at once, so naming and asking become a single action rather than two separate ones.
From a root for turning aside, related to the word for a grave niche cut off to one side. It describes bending a name away from its proper direction rather than denying it outright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names carried power in Arabia. A person's name announced lineage and often obligation, oaths were sworn by names, and poets attacked enemies by twisting theirs. Deities were addressed with strings of titles, and knowing the right form of address was thought to affect whether an appeal was heard. Instruction about which names to use was practical religious advice, not a matter of style.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never gives a closed list of these names. The phrase occurs four times, always in the same form, and the familiar lists compiled later were drawn from across the whole text by scholars rather than presented anywhere as a single passage. The number most often cited comes from a report rather than from the Quran itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge of God is presented as words given for use, not as information to be held. The instruction is to call. That makes the names tools of connection rather than items of doctrine. The handling of opponents is notably light. Distortion is named as a real fault and then left alone, with no correction demanded. The matter is placed between them and God, not in a dispute to be won.

crossReferences.why: Runs a long sequence of the names, closing with the same phrase used here.
Says either name may be used in calling, since the beautiful names belong to Him.
States the same phrase as a single sentence about the one worthy of worship.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the divine names you rarely think about and use it once a day this week when you ask for something, choosing it to fit what you are actually asking for. The verse joins naming to asking. Most people default to two or three names, and the difference a different one makes is worth noticing.
studies.explainEasier: The most beautiful names belong to God, so call on him using them. Leave alone the people who twist his names. They will get back what they have earned.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Drawn On By Degrees
studies.meaning: Four short ayat and each does a different job. The first names a community that guides by truth, using the same words applied earlier in this surah to a particular people. The second describes a drawing on step by step, from a direction they do not notice, which is what the verb literally means. The third adds a lengthening of the rope. The fourth turns to the audience and asks whether they have not reflected, pointing out that the man they are dismissing is their own companion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh explanation for the recitation was that the man producing it was possessed, which was the standard account of anyone who spoke in an unusual register. The ayah answers by reminding them that they had known him all his life, which is an argument from familiarity rather than from evidence. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: Built from the word for a step or rung. It describes bringing someone down a stair so gradually that no single step registers, which is why the ayah adds that they will not know the direction it comes from.
From a root for extension in time, related to the word for a long stretch of days. It names giving more rope rather than withholding a consequence, and its object is duration.
The ordinary word for someone you keep company with. The Quran uses it of the Prophet when addressing people who had known him for decades, so the term itself is the argument being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tethered animal given more rope grazes further out and does not notice the change; the herdsman lengthens it a hand's breadth at a time. Arabs used this deliberately with animals they wanted to keep calm. The vocabulary of both ayat here belongs to that practice, and to a listener who had let out a rope himself it described a process rather than a threat.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording of the first of these four ayat is identical to a sentence used earlier in this surah about one particular community. Here it is applied to those God created, with no people named at all. The Quran repeats the phrase without variation, so the same description does duty once for a specific group and once for humanity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a danger that has no unpleasant symptoms. Being drawn on by degrees and being given length are both experienced as things going well, which removes the usual signal that something needs attention. Set against that, the community named in the first ayah is defined by two activities, guiding and doing justice, both of which are outward and checkable, which is the Quran's usual answer to the problem of an unreliable inner sense.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical wording earlier in this surah, applied to a community among the people of Moses.
Repeats the same two verbs together, drawing on by steps and giving length, in the same order.
Describes doors of everything opened until they rejoiced, and then a sudden seizure.

studies.applyIt: Ask what has been going quietly well for you for a long time, and whether you have examined it lately. Not out of superstition. Simply because the passage points out that nothing about a comfortable stretch prompts anyone to look. Pick one such area and give it an hour of honest attention this week.

studies.title: Look Into The Dominion
studies.meaning: The question invites an act of looking, and the word for what is to be looked into is an intensified form of the ordinary noun for kingship, so it names the deep structure of things rather than their surface. Two objects are then joined: the dominion, and whatever God has created of anything, which widens the invitation to include everything. A third clause changes register entirely, asking whether their own term may have drawn near. The passage sets an enormous view and a personal deadline in one sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran's argument in this period rested heavily on observation, since the audience accepted a creator and disputed everything that followed from Him. Asking them to look was therefore not a demand for faith but a request that they finish an inference they had already begun. No occasion of revelation is reported. The second ayah closes the passage on those who are left in their overstepping.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the ordinary word for kingship, with an ending that adds weight and scope. It names the whole ordering behind what appears, which is why the verb attached to it is one of looking into rather than at.
The particle of possibility again, holding the clause short of a claim. What is raised is not that the term is near but that it may be, which is the only honest form such a statement can take.
A verb for moving without direction, used of someone confused in open country. It differs from the ordinary word for straying by naming the disorientation rather than the wrong road.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel made the sky an instrument rather than a view. A guide read stars for direction and season, and the whole calendar of markets, pilgrimage and rain followed from what was overhead. Looking up was work. The invitation in this ayah asks people who already looked at the sky every night to look into it once, which is a different verb and a different activity.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the dominion here is not the ordinary Arabic term for a kingdom. It carries an intensifying ending that Arabic adds to a small number of nouns to give them scope and grandeur, and the Quran uses this particular form only a few times, always of what lies behind the visible order rather than of any rule exercised within it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two scales are placed in one sentence and the join is the point. An invitation to consider everything that exists is followed immediately by a question about how much time the person considering it has left. Neither works alone: the vast view without the deadline becomes a pastime, and the deadline without the view becomes fear. Held together they produce the attention the surah has been asking for throughout.

crossReferences.why: Describes Abraham being shown the same deep dominion, using the identical unusual word for it.
Joins looking at the heavens and the earth with remembrance, and calls the result reflection.
Instructs looking at what is in the heavens and the earth, while noting that signs do not suffice alone.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week and look up for two minutes with the second question in mind rather than the first. Not how large is this, but how much time do I have. Most people do one or the other. The ayah puts them in a single sentence, and holding both at once for two minutes is the exercise.

studies.title: When Will It Anchor
studies.meaning: The question they ask uses a nautical word, asking when the Hour will drop anchor, and the answer is given twice in the same ayah with almost identical wording. Its knowledge is with my Lord. Its knowledge is with God. Between the two comes a description rather than a date: it weighs heavily on the heavens and the earth, and it will come only suddenly. Commentators differ over the word describing how they ask, reading it as though the Prophet were well-informed about it, or as though he were eager for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh asked for a date repeatedly, and the demand functioned as a challenge rather than an enquiry, since an unanswered question could be presented as a failure. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. The Quran's answer across the period was consistent, refusing the date while insisting on the event, and this is the fullest version of that refusal.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a ship coming to rest and for a mountain standing firm. The question asks when the Hour will drop anchor, which pictures it as something already at sea and approaching.
The ordinary verb for being heavy. Applied to the heavens and the earth it says the Hour presses on the whole created order, which is a statement about its magnitude rather than about its timing.
A rare adjective. Commentators read it as one who has enquired until he knows, or as one who is persistently keen, and both senses fit the sentence, which is why the tradition records the range.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan merchants knew ships from the Red Sea ports even if they rarely sailed. A vessel's arrival could not be predicted; you knew it was coming and you did not know the day, and the whole trading season turned on waiting for it. The word the questioners use belongs to that world, and it already concedes the arrival while asking only about the timing.
studies.didYouKnow: The same answer is given twice within one ayah, with only the divine name changed: its knowledge is with my Lord, and then its knowledge is with God. The Quran rarely repeats a clause so closely in a single ayah, and classical commentators read the repetition as closing the question rather than as emphasis for its own sake.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to give a date is not a gap in the message but part of it. A known date would convert preparation into scheduling, and the Quran removes that possibility while insisting the event is real and heavy. The description that replaces the date is also carefully chosen: suddenness is the one feature that has practical consequences, since it is the only thing about the timing that changes how a person should live now.

crossReferences.why: Lists knowledge of the Hour among the things held with God alone, beside four other matters.
Records the same question and the same answer, that its knowledge is with God alone.
Asks about its anchoring in the same words and says the messenger is only a warner for whoever fears it.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your planning assumes a length of life you have never been told. This is not a reason to plan less; the ayah does not say so. It is a reason to check whether anything important in your life is waiting for a stage that has no guaranteed arrival. Move one such thing forward this month.

studies.title: I Hold No Power
studies.meaning: The instruction is to say something that removes a claim rather than making one. I hold no benefit or harm for myself, except what God wills. Then an argument that is startling for its ordinariness: if I knew the unseen I would have acquired much good and no harm would have touched me. The reasoning is that a man with such knowledge would visibly prosper, and the speaker's own life is offered as evidence that he has none. The role is then stated in two words, a warner and a bearer of good news.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demands being made of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) included predictions, dates and the production of wonders, and the Quran's answers throughout this period narrow rather than expand the claims made for him. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes directly after the refusal to name a date, and it explains why that refusal was not an evasion.

keyTerms.note: The verb for owning and having disposal over something. The denial is about capacity rather than willingness, and its object is his own benefit and harm, which is the narrowest possible scope.

A form meaning to seek to increase one's share of something. The word is entirely ordinary and commercial, which is what makes the argument work: anyone with such knowledge would have done exactly this.
Two intensive forms naming the whole of the role. Both are about delivering information in advance, one unwelcome and one welcome, and neither implies any power over what is delivered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had men who claimed exactly what is being denied here. Soothsayers were consulted before journeys and marriages and were paid for it, and a reputation for foreknowledge made a man wealthy. The audience knew what such a person's life looked like. The argument in this ayah invites them to compare that picture with the man in front of them, which was an argument they could check without leaving the city.
studies.didYouKnow: The reasoning offered is an argument from ordinary self-interest, and it is put in the first person about the Prophet himself. Anyone who knew the unseen would have used it to acquire more and to avoid harm, so a life without those advantages is evidence of not having it. The Quran rarely argues in this register, and here it does so about its own messenger.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a firm boundary around what a messenger is. He is not a source of benefit or protection, not for others and not for himself, and the exception clause attaches whatever he does have to God's will rather than to his standing. That leaves the message as the whole of what he brings, which is why the Quran can attach so much to following him while attaching nothing to petitioning him.

crossReferences.why: Has him say he holds no harm or right guidance for anyone, and that none could protect him.
Denies knowledge of the unseen and possession of treasuries, and denies being an angel.
Applies the same disclaimer to himself before answering a question about the appointed term.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are quietly acting as though you knew how something will turn out. The investment, the conversation you are avoiding, the person you have decided will not change. You do not know. Say that plainly about one of them today and see what becomes possible once the assumed knowledge is set down.

studies.title: That He Might Find Rest
studies.meaning: The purpose named for the pair is stillness. The verb comes from the root for dwelling and coming to rest, the same one used earlier in this surah for settling in the Garden, so companionship is described by the quiet it produces rather than by anything it achieves. Then a pregnancy told in three short movements: a light burden, carried on with, and then heaviness. At that point they call, and the call is a promise. If You give us a sound child, we will be among the thankful.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical commentators divide over whether this passage speaks of the first human pair or of husbands and wives generally, and both readings are old. Those who read it of the first pair rely largely on reports the commentators themselves identify as coming from Israelite tradition, and Ibn Kathir treats them with caution. The general reading takes the singular as covering every couple.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness and dwelling, the same one behind the word for tranquillity. The purpose named is not company or offspring but the settling of a restlessness, which is a specific claim.

The word for burden covers both a load and a pregnancy. Calling it light names the early stage precisely, when it is real and barely felt, which the following verb about carrying on with it completes.
The verb for becoming weighty, and the exact opposite of the adjective used a clause earlier. The Arabic marks the whole passage of a pregnancy by moving from one word to its antonym.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childbirth in seventh-century Arabia was dangerous and the danger was known to everyone. Women died, infants died, and a family counted its surviving children rather than its births. The prayer described here, made at the point where the pregnancy becomes undeniable, was the ordinary response of people who had no other recourse, and it would have been recognised by every listener as their own household's prayer.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic tracks a pregnancy by moving from one adjective to its opposite. It is first a light burden, and then the verb used says she became heavy, built from the antonym of the first word. Two words separated by a single clause carry the whole passage of time, without any months or stages being named.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The purpose given for marriage is rest rather than function, which is unusual in a religious text and generous towards ordinary life. The passage then shows a couple praying at the moment of vulnerability and making a promise, and the ayat that follow describe the promise not being kept. That sequence, which is the Quran's steady interest, matters more than the identification of the couple that the commentators dispute.

crossReferences.why: Names the same purpose using the same root, and adds affection and mercy placed between them.
The next ayah, which reports what was done once the prayer had been answered.
Describes a pregnancy and its hardship, ending in a prayer of thanks rather than a promise.

studies.applyIt: If you are married, ask whether your household is a place either of you actually rests. Not whether it functions. Rest is the word the ayah uses, and it is easy to run a working household in which nobody has been still for a year. Change one thing this week that makes the evening quieter rather than more productive.

studies.title: Partners In What Was Given
studies.meaning: The gift arrives and partners are assigned in it, which is the precise wrong being named: not partners in general but partners in the very thing that was just granted. Commentators divide over who is described, some reading the first human pair and others reading parents generally, and those who take the first reading rely largely on reports they identify as coming from Israelite tradition. The ayat that follow shift to the plural and argue the case: things that create nothing and are themselves created, and cannot help anyone, including themselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabs commonly attached a newborn's safe arrival to a shrine, a saint or a vow made at a particular place, and names were given that recorded the debt. The Quran addresses this practice without naming anyone, and the argument that follows is general rather than local. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat, and the plural forms in the second and third make the address wider than any one couple.

keyTerms.note: From a root for sharing a property or a herd. What is described is the assigning of a share in something to someone who had no part in producing it, which is why the ayah adds the phrase in what He gave them.

A verb of height used in the Quran to place God beyond a description just mentioned. It closes the sentence by stating a distance rather than by refuting the claim, which is the Book's usual move here.
A passive clause set immediately after an active one. The Arabic puts making and being made in the same breath, so the argument is finished by grammar before any reasoning is added to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vows attached to childbirth were ordinary across Arabia. A woman who conceived after long waiting might promise a sacrifice at a particular shrine, or dedicate the child's name to whatever was venerated there, and the whole family understood the arrangement as a debt properly paid. Nothing about it felt like a betrayal. That ordinariness is precisely the condition these ayat address.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage begins in the dual, describing two people, and then moves to the plural for the argument that follows. Classical commentators note the shift and divide over what it indicates, some reading it as a move from one couple to their descendants and others as a sign that the general sense was intended from the start. Both readings are preserved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wrong identified is very specific: a share is assigned in the exact thing that was given. That is a failure of accounting rather than of belief, and it can happen to people who would name God correctly if asked. The argument that follows is equally practical, testing candidates by what they can do rather than by what they are, and finding that they cannot even help themselves.

crossReferences.why: Describes turning to God in distress and then assigning a share to others once relief arrives.
Uses the same argument, that they create nothing and are themselves created, and hold no power.
Shows a person calling on his Lord in distress and then setting up rivals once favoured.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for and received. Now notice who or what gets the credit in the story you tell about it: your timing, a contact, good luck, a particular person's help. Some of that credit is accurate. Just check whether any of it was quietly moved off the original account, and move it back.

studies.title: It Is The Same Either Way
studies.meaning: Two ayat and both turn on the verb for calling. If you call them to guidance they will not follow, and then a flat statement: it makes no difference whether you call them or keep silent. The second ayah gives the reason, and it is the sharpest sentence in the passage. Those you call upon are servants like yourselves. Then the invitation, phrased as a test anyone can run. Call them, and let them answer you, if what you say is true.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city whose whole religious economy ran on appeals made at a sanctuary. The Quran's argument here is not that the appeals are wrong in principle but that the addressees are of the same order as the people addressing them. No occasion of revelation is reported. These ayat close the surah's argument before its final instructions, and they are cast as a challenge rather than an assertion.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used throughout the Quran for supplication. Using it for both the calling of people to guidance and the calling upon objects lets the two ayat turn on one word held in two senses.

The participle for one who says nothing. Its use here is stark, since the ayah says the outcome is identical whether or not anything is said, which is the strongest way of describing a call that goes nowhere.
Two words that finish the argument. Whatever is being appealed to is placed in the same category as the person appealing, which removes the difference in standing that any appeal requires.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Appeals in Arabia went upward through a chain of standing. You asked a stronger man because he had something you did not, and the whole system of clients and patrons rested on that difference being real. To be told that the party you were appealing to was in exactly your own position was not a religious objection to that audience. It was a statement that the transaction could not work.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran closes this passage by inviting a test that anyone can perform. Call them, and let them answer you. Classical commentators note that the Book uses this form of argument repeatedly, offering a check rather than a proof, and always in a way that costs the challenger nothing to attempt and can be attempted immediately.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage reasons about supplication in terms of the addressee rather than the asker. Sincerity, urgency and repetition make no difference if the party called upon is of the same order as the caller, which is why the ayah says silence and speech produce the same result. That places the whole weight of prayer on who is being addressed, and it is the reason the Quran spends so much more time on that question than on technique.

crossReferences.why: Compares such calling to a man stretching his hands to water that will never reach his mouth.
Says they do not hear the call, and could not answer it if they did, and will disown it later.
Gives the positive counterpart, an invitation to call with a promise of an answer attached.

studies.applyIt: Look at where you take your worries first. For most people it is a person, a search bar, or a plan. None of those is wrong. But notice the order, and try putting a short direct prayer at the front of it once this week, before the other steps rather than after they have failed.

studies.title: Feet To Walk With
studies.meaning: Four questions in a row, each naming a faculty and the action it exists for. Feet to walk with, hands to grip with, eyes to see with, ears to hear with. The list is the mirror of one given a few ayat earlier, where human beings were described as possessing exactly these and not using them. Here the objects lack them altogether. Then the closing challenge, spoken with striking confidence: call your partners, then scheme against me and grant me no respite.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the challenge at the end was made in a city where the speaker had no protection beyond his own clan and was in real danger. Its force came from being issued by someone with nothing to fall back on. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It closes the surah's argument about what may be called upon, immediately before the statement of where the speaker's own protection lies.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking hold with force, used of a hand closing on something to move or strike it. It names what hands are for in terms of power rather than of dexterity, which fits a list about capability.

An imperative from the root for laying a plan unseen. Inviting people to plot against you is a challenge that only makes sense if you believe their planning has no reach, which is the point being made.
From the root for looking, and therefore for granting a delay. The same verb appeared at the start of this surah in a request for respite, and here it is a refusal to be granted any.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The images at Arabian shrines were made things with a maker's marks on them. People washed them, dressed them, carried them on journeys and repaired them when they cracked. Everyone who venerated one had also, at some point, lifted it. The questions in this ayah do not tell the audience anything they did not know; they simply ask them to say out loud what they had handled with their own hands.
studies.didYouKnow: This list is the exact counterpart of one a few ayat earlier in the same surah. There, people are described as having hearts, eyes and ears and not using them. Here, objects are asked whether they have feet, hands, eyes and ears at all. The Quran sets unused faculties beside absent ones within one surah and lets the comparison stand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test applied is functional throughout. Nothing is said about what these objects are made of or who made them; the questions ask only what they can do, and the list is of the most basic capacities any living thing has. Setting that beside the earlier description of human beings who possess these faculties and do not use them raises a harder question, which the surah leaves the reader holding.

crossReferences.why: The counterpart list earlier in this surah, of faculties possessed and left unused.
Abraham asks the same kind of question, whether they benefit or harm those who serve them.
Offers a similar test, that all of them together could not create a fly or retrieve from it.

studies.applyIt: Take the four faculties named here and check which of yours are actually in service today. Feet that go somewhere worth going, hands that hold something worth holding, eyes and ears used on a person rather than a screen. Pick the one that has been idle longest and use it once, deliberately, before the day ends.

studies.title: My Protector Is God
studies.meaning: The declaration is personal and it is grounded in a specific act: my protector is God, who sent down the Book. The relationship is identified by what has been given rather than by any general claim, and the second clause widens it, saying He takes charge of the righteous. Then the contrast, and it is given twice with a small variation. Those you call besides Him cannot help you and cannot help themselves. You may call them to guidance and they do not hear, and you see them looking at you and not seeing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the word used here for a protector is the same one the surah opened with, in a warning against taking such figures besides God. The Book closes its argument by returning to the term it began with and naming its one legitimate holder. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat, which stand just before the surah's final instructions.

keyTerms.note: The singular of the word this surah opened by warning against taking besides God. The whole chapter runs between a prohibition of false patrons and this declaration of the true one.
The verb from the same root, so the sentence uses one root twice: He is my patron, and He acts as patron to the righteous. Protection is described as something exercised rather than merely held.
The ordinary verb for directing the eyes at something, set immediately against a denial of seeing. Arabic can hold both, since one word names the direction of a gaze and the other its result.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's patron was the most consequential fact about him. Protection was declared publicly, and it determined whether he could travel, trade or expect redress if he were harmed. When a patron withdrew it, the man was exposed overnight. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) lived through exactly that transition in Mecca, and the declaration in this ayah was made by someone who knew what the word cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The final image describes carved figures with eyes turned towards the viewer, looking and not seeing. Craftsmen shaped and painted them precisely so the gaze would meet a worshipper's, which is what makes the description so exact. The ayah does not deny the appearance. It grants the appearance and denies what everyone assumed was behind it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection is defined by capacity rather than by devotion. The test applied is whether the party appealed to can act, and it is applied even to their own case: those who cannot help themselves cannot help anyone. Against that, the declaration names a protector identified by something already delivered, so the claim rests on an act that has taken place rather than on an assurance about the future.

crossReferences.why: Opens this surah by warning against following patrons besides Him, using the same word.
Names God as the patron of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light.
Asks whether they have taken protectors besides Him, when God is the protector who gives life.

studies.applyIt: Write down who you would call first if something serious went wrong tonight. That list is real and worth having. Then ask what each name on it can actually do, and where their capacity ends. Naming the limit does not diminish anyone. It just makes visible the gap this ayah is describing.

studies.title: Take What Comes Easily
studies.meaning: Three instructions arrive in one line, and the first is the most discussed. The word can mean pardon, or what is spare and easily given. So early scholars read it as accepting what people readily offer rather than pressing them. They also read it as forgiving. A warning about provocation follows, with a practical response: take refuge. Then comes a description of those aware of God. They remember and then see clearly, unlike those who are dragged on without stopping.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the end of a long surah. That surah has run through the destruction of earlier communities and the arguments of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with his own people. These closing instructions are addressed to him about how to conduct that argument. Early scholars record several reports about the first verse. All of them turn on how a person deals with those who will not listen.

keyTerms.note: The root covers both forgiving and surplus. Early scholars take it here as accepting what people offer without pressing them to their limit, which is why the same word can also mean pardon.
Not the uninformed. The word names people who act without restraint, and older poetry uses it for hot-headedness, so avoiding them means declining a fight rather than avoiding the uneducated.
A sudden jab, the word used of driving an animal forward with a point. It names the suggestion as brief and external rather than as a settled state, which is why the response given is immediate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab honour culture required an answer to every provocation. Skilled opponents provoked on purpose, knowing that an angry man could be steered into a costly quarrel. Poets baited each other in public for exactly that reason. Turning away read as weakness. The instruction to decline the exchange was not passive advice in that setting. It cut against the main engine of social standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to take refuge is followed in the very next verse by an account of what taking refuge looks like from the inside. A person remembers, and then sees. Classical scholars follow that sequence closely. The passage moves from an outward command to an inward description of it working, which is unusual in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats provocation as something that happens to a person, not as something they are. That distinction does a great deal of work. The sudden impulse is described as a jab from outside. The response asked for is not suppression but relocation, taking shelter somewhere. And the contrast at the end is not between good people and bad. It is between those who notice and those who are pulled along without ever stopping.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with a reason, repelling harm with what is better.
Describes the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with peace.
Preserves a supplication for refuge from the promptings of devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time you feel the sharp pull to answer something, name it as a jab rather than as your own opinion. Wait until you have finished one slow breath.
