The passage puts a specific move in that gap. It does not say the provocation was unreal. It says the response is a place you go rather than a thing you win.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to take what people give easily. He is to ask for what is right, and to keep away from rude people. If a bad thought jabs at you, ask God to keep you safe.

studies.title: Listen, And Be Silent
studies.meaning: A demand is reported and refused. When no sign is produced, the opponents suggest he should simply have made one up. The reply concedes nothing about his own resources. He follows what is revealed, and does not compose. The text then names itself as insight, guidance and mercy. The second verse turns to the listener with two instructions, hearing and silence. It attaches an outcome to them that is left as a hope rather than a promise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah. The demand for a produced sign runs through the whole Meccan period. Early scholars connect the second verse with how people behaved during recitation, though the reports vary: some link it to the prayer, others to any occasion of hearing. What the two verses share is a shift from arguing about the Quran to describing how it is to be received.

keyTerms.note: A verb for picking something out and gathering it for yourself. The taunt assumes composition, so the choice of word makes the accusation precise: they are asking him to produce, not to transmit.
The plural of a word for inner sight, formed like an instrument. It names the text as something you see by rather than something you look at, which is why the verse pairs it with guidance.
A verb specifically for stopping your own speech in order to hear. It is added after the command to listen, so attention and silence are named separately and each is asked for on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was heard, not read. Audiences at the fairs listened with a critical ear and interrupted freely. Recitation was public and competitive. A listener's noise was itself a form of judgement. Reports describe opponents at Mecca urging one another to drown out the recitation with talk and clamour. Telling listeners to fall silent addressed a real tactic, not merely a matter of manners.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the places in the Quran where the text describes the right behaviour towards itself. The surah ends two verses later with a prostration. It is one of the passages at which readers traditionally prostrate during recitation. So the instruction to listen is followed at once by an instruction the body carries out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to produce a sign on demand defines prophecy by what it excludes. The messenger's role leaves out invention. Admitting that publicly costs him the argument in the short term. The passage then moves the evidence into the text itself. It calls the text insight rather than proof. And the instruction to listen implies something is passed on in the hearing that cannot be got by discussing it afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand to alter the Quran and the same refusal to change it.
Lists the specific signs demanded of him and the answer given to them.
Describes what happens to believers when the verses are recited to them.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the Quran recited, whether you follow the words or not, stop what you are doing for the length of one passage and give it nothing but attention. No phone, no half-listening. The verse asks for two separate things, hearing and silence, and most of us have got out of the habit of the second.
studies.explainEasier: People asked the Prophet to make up a sign of his own. He said he only follows what God sends him. When the Quran is read out, listen and stay quiet, and mercy may come to you.

studies.title: Within Yourself, Not Aloud
studies.meaning: The instruction has five parts and four of them are about manner rather than content. Remember your Lord within yourself; humbly; with awe; below the raising of the voice; morning and evening. The word for humility here shares its root with the verb used earlier in this surah for what hardship is meant to produce, so the posture the ayah asks for is the one difficulty produces on its own. The closing clause is a warning against the condition the whole surah has been naming.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Public devotion in the sanctuary was loud and performed in front of others, and the early Muslims prayed under observation and sometimes under pressure. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It comes near the very end of the surah, after every argument has been made, and it turns from what to think to how to hold it, which is how the chapter closes.

keyTerms.note: From a root for smallness and abasement. The same root appeared earlier in this surah as the purpose hardship serves, so what is instructed here is the posture that difficulty otherwise has to produce.
A noun for a quiet, inward apprehension rather than fright. It is placed beside humility as a pair, so what is asked for is a manner with two components rather than one intensified feeling.
A phrase specifying a level rather than silence. Something is being said, and it is being said under the volume that others would hear, which is a description of privacy rather than of soundlessness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Worship at the sanctuary was audible and communal. Clans chanted their own formulas as they circled, and the noise was part of the occasion; a person praying silently would have been conspicuous. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the early believers often prayed in the outskirts to avoid interference. The instruction here describes a devotion that leaves no trace for anyone else to observe or interrupt.
studies.didYouKnow: The two times named, the morning and the evening, are the hinges of the day rather than its middle. Arabic marks them with a pair of words that appear together across the Quran, and the pairing is always about the beginning and closing of a stretch of activity rather than about any particular hour within it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is almost entirely about manner, which is unusual for a passage about remembrance. Nothing is specified to say. What is specified is where it happens, in what bearing, at what volume and when, and the effect is to describe something that cannot be performed for an audience. The final clause then names inattention as the thing being guarded against, which is the condition the whole surah has diagnosed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction earlier in this surah, to call humbly and in secret, using the same root.
Sets the same middle level of voice, neither loud in prayer nor silent, but a way between.
Names what this produces, hearts settling in the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Take thirty seconds at the start and end of tomorrow, before the phone and after it goes down, and say something to God under your breath. Not a formula unless you want one. The ayah specifies the manner and leaves the words open, and the two times it names are the two nobody else has a claim on.

studies.title: They Are Not Too Proud
studies.meaning: The surah ends by describing those who are with your Lord, whom the commentators identify as the angels. Three things are said of them and the first is a denial. They are not too great for His service, which uses the same verb the surah applied to its very first refusal, at the beginning of the chapter. Then they glorify Him, and then, in a clause with its object placed first for emphasis, to Him they bow down. The whole surah closes on the act the whole surah opened by describing being refused.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Angels were part of the religious landscape the audience already accepted, and some Arabs regarded them as daughters of God or as intermediaries whose favour could be sought. The Quran consistently describes them as servants instead, which is what this closing ayah does. No occasion of revelation is reported. It is the last ayah of the surah and the whole chapter turns on it.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used for the first refusal at the opening of this surah, in the same reflexive form. The chapter's last ayah denies of the angels exactly what its first narrative reported of another.
From a root for swimming or moving freely through something. To glorify in this vocabulary is to declare God clear of every deficiency, so the act is a removal rather than an addition.

keyTerms.gloss: and to Him they bow down
keyTerms.note: The object is placed before its verb, which in Arabic restricts it: to Him and to no one else. The chapter's final word is the same verb refused in its opening narrative.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs venerated intermediaries and expected them to carry a petition upward, and several of the figures at the sanctuary were understood in something like those terms. Approaching a great person through someone with access was simply how anything was done. A closing ayah that describes the highest beings as servants who bow rather than as agents who intercede removed the whole mechanism the audience relied on.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the first place in the Quran's order where the reciter and the listener bow down, and the tradition has treated it as such from the earliest period. The surah that opened with a refusal to bow therefore ends by prompting the act it began by describing being withheld, and it does so at the moment the chapter closes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah's structure completes itself in a single sentence. It opened with a command to bow refused out of self-magnifying, spent two hundred ayat on communities who refused messengers for the same reason, and ends by describing beings who are not too great for service and who bow. Nothing is argued in the last ayah; the chapter simply supplies the alternative and leaves the reader in a position to take it.

crossReferences.why: The refusal this closing ayah answers, at the opening of the same surah, in the same vocabulary.
Describes those with Him as not too proud for His service, glorifying night and day without flagging.
Says all in the heavens and earth bow, and that they fear their Lord above them and do as commanded.

studies.applyIt: Read the surah's first few ayat and this last one together, in one sitting. It takes four minutes. The chapter is built as an arc between a refusal and a bowing, and reading only the ends of it is the quickest way to feel what the two hundred ayat in between are actually for.
